In highly anisotropic materials, a specific type of magnetic response, induced by Pauli paramagnetism, can be significant. This response is triggered by the interaction between superconducting waves and normal electrons under the influence of an external magnetic field. Typically, in superconductors with triplet pairing, this response is minimal due to an inherent imbalance between the pairs' orbital and magnetic moments. However, when the pairing is in a mixed state of two distinct components that respond differently to a magnetic field, a larger Pauli paramagnetic response can result. This principle has been shown to apply in materials with this type of mixed triplet pairing, such as in a specific class of topologically ordered materials called nematic superconductors. As such, the coexistence of two distinct pairing components and spin polarization necessary for a substantial Pauli paramagnetic response to occur limits the accessibility of this phenomenon. We propose a new framework for machine learning, which integrates a game-like component between the learner and a teacher. The learner's goal is to accurately classify a given dataset, while the teacher deliberately tries to make this task harder by selectively labeling a subset of the data as target classes. When the dataset and target classes are drawn from a known distribution of possible scenarios, called the strategy space, our approach ensures that the learner's accuracy remains within predetermined limits by choosing an optimal response to any possible teacher action. If the actual distribution of data and target classes differs from the strategy space, we demonstrate that the minimax approach can identify and adapt to this variation with an accurate model of the teacher's behavior. This adaptability allows our system to achieve better results than other machine learning methods on a range of tasks, including supervised classification, unsupervised clustering, and active learning. Our code is available online at https://github.com/PlatypusTech/MinimaxLearner. Our approach is also related to studies of how a learner might interact with a cheating teacher in the field of algorithmic learning theory. This framework provides a more comprehensive understanding of the learner's abilities in this scenario, while our implementation of the minimax approach is the first to successfully engage in two-way interactions between the learner and teacher. Further research is needed to explore the broader applications of this framework. Specifically, we see potential for our system to improve the accuracy of models trained on semi-supervised, transfer learning, and online data. Our methodology can serve as a starting point for these tasks, with a theoretical guarantee that our approach will achieve better results than other machine learning methods. Our code is designed to be flexible and adaptable, with features such as data augmentation, feature selection, and active learning already integrated and easily customizable. Our approach is also grounded in fundamental principles of how a learner might interact with a teacher in the fields of epistemic economics and learning theory, while our findings on adapting to different distributions of data and target classes are new contributions to these areas. Our system can be applied to a wide range of domains, with specific examples including natural language processing, computer vision, and reinforcement learning. To study the dynamics of musical complexity, we calculated the self-information of song lengths in the Million Song Dataset from 1922 to 2011, showing that length variability decreased over time. We then used this information to construct a universe of all possible song lengths, ranging from one to 451 seconds, and calculated the relative probability of songs within a specified length range. The relative probability initially decreases as song lengths increase, becoming more nonlinear and complex, eventually leveling out due to the physical constraints of human perception. By modeling the relative probability with a power law, we found an exponent change point around the 1990s, indicating a shift towards more homogeneous song lengths in recent decades. This change may be attributed to digital music production and the influence of pop music on musical complexity. To further investigate song length patterns, we applied the Zipf law to song lengths and found that the law's exponent decreased over time, suggesting a change in the distribution of song lengths among different genres. Our work demonstrates how information theory can be used to analyze musical complexity and discover unexpected patterns in data. The methods employed in this study can be applied to other areas of research, such as bioinformatics, where identifying pattern distributions can shed new light on underlying processes. Ultimately, this research may contribute to a theory of musical complexity that can inform the creation of more aesthetically pleasing music. Additionally, our findings highlight the significance of considering both absolute and relative probability in scientific studies, as the two can vary greatly in real-world data. By combining absolute and relative probability, we can gain a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying processes that shape our environment. Finally, while our research may lack personal value, it is a valuable example of a low-cost, high-throughput project that can be completed in under two weeks, demonstrating the potential of information theory and machine learning to uncover new insights in various fields of study. Therefore, we are releasing our code and dataset under a free license, hoping that our study will contribute to the development of novel machine learning algorithms and new theories in musical complexity. In the future, we plan to extend our research by applying our methods to other datasets and studying the informational complexity of other artistic creations. By analyzing data on a large scale, we can gain a more objective understanding of artistic processes and test the idea that artistic complexity evolves over time, eventually leading to more aesthetically pleasing works. Ultimately, this research may help us develop algorithms for automated artistic generation, enabling computers to produce innovative and complex music, art, literature, and other forms of creative content.

A new set of out-of-distribution detection methods for natural language processing called NLP-OOD has emerged, which distinguishes between different types of out-of-distribution text rather than simply identifying a general out-of-the-way text.  We should consider whether one day these sophisticated methods will be utilized in high-stakes environments such as law.  Initially, these sophisticated methods were not as effective as general-purpose techniques, but with the advancement of language models, they have shown improved performance.  However, despite progress, these sophisticated methods still struggle with certain types of out-of-distribution text, including those that are semantically similar but syntactically distant.  Therefore, it is crucial to conduct thorough assessments to guarantee the reliability of these sophisticated methods in real-world scenarios.  We have created a comprehensive dataset with 14 categories of out-of-distribution text and a detailed evaluation process that accounts for data redundancy, ensuring that each category is uniquely represented across various datasets.  This research provides a thorough analysis of the performance of these sophisticated methods, as well as a comparative study with previous approaches, highlighting the reliance of these methods on pre-trained language models and the difficulty of handling questions that require semantic understanding.  This research introduces novel benchmarks in question-answering and sentiment analysis that go beyond the basic out-of-distribution text challenge, requiring models to grapple with the complexities of the target category.  This research demonstrates the potential for improved results by combining sophisticated out-of-distribution text detection methods with data augmentation and domain adaptation techniques.  The proposed approach has been successfully evaluated on 15 datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in 12 cases, and outperforming current state-of-the-art models by 3.4% overall.  This research will be made available to the public, enabling further exploration and improvement.  This paper will be presented at the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Natural Language Processing, where we will share our research with the NLP-OOD community and potentially inspire future work in this area.  This paper has been accepted with distinction at the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Natural Language Processing.  Two peer reviewers commended the research for its thorough evaluation process, the introduction of novel benchmarks, and the substantial improvement achieved through developed approaches. By eliminating the need for a predefined hyperplane, this approach can effectively handle complex nonlinear problems while adapting to an optimal regression surface for accurate component extraction. Destructive events like earthquakes are causing significant disruptions to urban areas due to aging infrastructure. The resulting fires and collapses are exacerbating a critical situation, prompting a massive exodus of people in need of emergency support. To address this, disaster relief efforts are spread across urban landscapes in the form of emergency shelters. Given the overwhelming demand, it is essential to optimize the distribution and flow of people across different locations to ensure effective disaster management. By transforming disaster scenarios into complex network systems, researchers can model and solve problems using sophisticated mathematical tools. A key challenge is developing methods for generating and updating these network maps in real-time, as urban environments are notoriously hard to model accurately. In response, scientists are turning to agent-based modeling, where individual agents are navigating dynamic network conditions. Although this approach shows promise, it is often limited by its focus on local interactions and the absence of external influences shaping the cityscape. In contrast, traffic management is another critical aspect of urban mobility receiving significant attention. A prominent traffic flow model known as the Aw-Rushton-Meyer model is well-suited for large-scale applications but lacks built-in mechanisms for handling disruptions. To bridge this gap, a new model is proposed that integrates traffic flow with collective motion, using local rules and network topology to generate coherent global patterns. A key innovation is the introduction of a variable measuring the attraction of different locations, paving the way for the emergence of macroscopic patterns observed in real-world traffic phenomena. A detailed analysis reveals how this model responds to external stimuli, such as earthquakes, and how disaster relief efforts are affected by changes in the city's landscape. To quantify this, a special type of network known as scale-free networks is used to model the distribution of emergency shelters, leading to the development of a novel equation describing the dynamics of these networks. A detailed study shows that even minor changes in the city's structure can lead to significant changes in the flow of people, highlighting the need for dynamic and adaptable response strategies. To test these ideas, a range of numerical simulations are conducted using a sophisticated software tool, confirming that agent-based modeling and traffic management approaches can be combined to tackle complex urban challenges. A key outcome is a set of design principles, providing scientists and engineers with practical guidelines for developing effective disaster response strategies and optimizing urban mobility. Additionally, a novel approach is proposed for generating and updating network maps in real-time, showcasing the potential applications of complex network models in urban mobility and disaster management. It is argued that agent-based modeling and traffic management are complementary approaches that can learn from each other,

Specifically, we show that complex numbers are not needed for describing quantum states, but rather can be incorporated through the use of Hermitian matrices with specific properties. Dark matter particle research has been conducted using a dataset of 35.9 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, collected by the CMS experiment. The study focuses on events where a pair of dark matter particles are created alongside a ritically decaying Z boson at mass 75.0 GeV, and is characterized by a distinct dipha jet signal under standard model conditions. Two analysis methods were employed: one using reconstructed Z boson kinematics and Rapidity, and the other using mass signatures at the Z boson peak. No significant results were found beyond standard model expectations, and statistical confidence limits were established for cross section measurements in the two scenarios. The absence of signal excess above background noise places constraints on the cross section of dark matter pairs as small as 45.7 fb and 27.6 fb for dark matter masses of 50 GeV and 125 GeV, respectively, well in line with theoretical models using simplified models of dark matter and a spin-0 mediator. The study provides the most stringent constraints to date on dark matter particle interactions via Z boson mediation. Furthermore, using specific coupling values of 10^-3 and dark matter mass of 125 GeV, the study excludes the existence of dark matter particles with mass less than approximately 250 GeV. This research extends the search for dark matter particles in proton-proton collisions, and the study's findings will guide theoretical models of dark matter interactions in future research. The study's data remains available in the CMS data repository. Research into remote epitaxy has regained momentum due to its potential to decrease the cost of device production by using cheap substrate alternatives.  Achieving successful remote epitaxy requires precise control over the equilibrium between different growth mechanisms, specifically remote epitaxy, pinhole epitaxy, and van der Waals epitaxy.  A theoretical study applied to the case of Co$_2$FeAl/Gr/sapphire found that the competition between these mechanisms is highly dependent on the remote epitaxy growth energy, which can be influenced by a foreign substrate's lattice parameter and surface energy.  Pinhole epitaxy becomes dominant when the energy barrier for island nucleation is lowered, while van der Waals epitaxy prevails when surface adhesion is increased.  A theoretical model was validated using first-principles calculations for Co$_2$FeAl/Gr/sapphire and compared with experimental results, providing an understanding of the remote epitaxy process and how to optimize growth conditions.  Modifying the chemical composition of Heusler alloys can also shift the equilibrium towards remote epitaxy, making these materials ideal candidates for investigating this promising technique.  Furthermore, these findings offer insights into the remote epitaxy process and can contribute to the development of more efficient and cost-effective material growth techniques.  These results could be applied to other materials with similar properties, such as Co$_2$MnAl, by adjusting their chemical composition to exploit the remote epitaxy mechanism.  Ultimately, this research could lead to the creation of high-performance devices using low-cost, flexible graphene substrates.  Graphene's unique properties, such as high conductivity and flexibility, make it an ideal substrate for these devices, allowing them to be bent without affecting their performance.  In conclusion, this research has provided a theoretical understanding of the remote epitaxy process and how it can be optimized, which is a crucial step towards developing this promising technique. To motivate network service providers (SPs) to enhance Quality of Service (QoS) for content providers (CPs), this study introduces a profit-sharing agreement. Under these contracts, SPs agree to improve QoS for a specified CP in return for a portion of the revenue generated by that CP. Our analysis examines various scenarios in which SPs and CPs negotiate fair contracts based on different assumptions about revenue and utility functions. We find a Nash Bargaining Solution (NBS) for all these scenarios, which we refer to as a Fair Profit-Sharing Contract (FPSC). Our analysis shows that FPSCs are unique, robust, and resilient to variations in revenue and utility function scaling factors. Moreover, FPSCs for multiple CPs can be realized through a combination of FPSCs for individual CPs. We illustrate the applicability of our results in a scenario involving an SP, a CP, and a mediator, which we call the Profits Manager (PM). Our findings are further exemplified in numerical simulations, which demonstrate how FPSCs can be successfully negotiated even when the PM's goals are conflicting with those of the SP and CP. Our work contributes to the existing literature by providing a theoretical framework, known as Profits Distribution Theory (PDT), which can be used to derive FPSCs. Ultimately, our research enables SPs and CPs to enter into contracts that result in improved network quality for CPs and a more equitable distribution of profits. The latter is effectuated through an FPSC that causes the SP's cost to decrease and the CP's cost to increase in proportion to the SP's profit-sharing fraction. This research innovates by introducing a novel, result-oriented approach to game theory, which prioritizes the FPSC's ability to effectuate a desirable outcome, rather than the FPSC itself. The research findings suggest that this mechanism has the potential to improve trust in online auctions by balancing the needs of bidders for fairness and the auctioneer for revenue. The outcome can be utilized to develop more robust and trustworthy auction designs for a variety of applications, including crowdsourcing, with the aim of increasing overall efficiency. Specifically, the mechanism has the potential to increase the overall revenue of a mechanism in scenarios of private, independent values. We initiate a study of local defining ideals of Hessenberg varieties, specifically focusing on regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties of type A, utilizing a new decomposition of the affine chart within the corresponding partial flag manifold. This decomposition, which exhibits remarkable symmetry, enables us to derive local defining ideals through geometric vertex decomposition and link them to Gröbner fans and arrangements of reflexive Hessenberg configurations. Consequently, this framework allows us to compute explicit equations for certain Hessenberg varieties, such as the regular nilpotent $Sp_{2n}$ Hessenberg variety of a specific shape and a particular Gröbner type, and also establish a connection between the regular nilpotent $Sp_4$ Hessenberg variety of yet another specific shape and Frobenius partitions. Moreover, this analysis paves the way for a comprehensive computation of the regular nilpotent $Sp_4$ Hessenberg variety of yet another specific shape and Frobenius partitions. Finally, this computational method resolves two previously unsolved instances in The Nilpotent Hessenberg Monodromy Problem as described in arXiv:1809.10785. Additionally, we make available a publicly viewable implementation of our computational methods in SymPy. In the event of a supernova explosion, neutrino flavor conversion can occur rapidly, potentially producing intense beams of low-energy neutrinos that could interact with nearby matter. This process is often accelerated by instabilities, particularly by the neutrino self-interaction effect. To better understand and predict this conversion, we studied neutrino flavor instabilities in detailed three-dimensional models of core-collapse supernovae. Our high-precision calculations in both axisymmetric and 3D simulations revealed various features of fast, or "mildly nonlinear," neutrino flavor instabilities. We found that in many cases, neutrino flavor instabilities are confined to limited regions, primarily due to the rapid growth triggered by the neutrino self-interaction effect. However, we also observed instances where the instabilities persist due to an imbalance in matter density and the resulting resonant axes alignment. Our findings indicate that, in some cases, the growth of neutrino flavor instabilities is hindered by non-axial velocities in the neutrino distribution, leading to stabilization. Our research provides new insights into the rapid neutrino flavor conversion process and its associated instabilities, ultimately contributing to more accurate modeling of rapid neutrino flavor conversion in supernovae. Our analysis also serves as a reference for future studies using the Lagrangean framework to investigate the dynamics of this process. Furthermore, we have established a standard method for evaluating and comparing the properties of neutrino flavor instabilities in various simulations, allowing for a deeper understanding of the underlying physics and a broader exploration of the parameter space, including variations in nuclear equation of state and nuclear pairing. Our research paves the way for more precise calculations of rapid neutrino flavor conversion, utilizing high-order methods in both the Eulerian and Lagrangean frameworks. These advancements will ultimately enable the determination of fast neutrino flavor conversion rates, ultimately influencing supernova pairness and explosion prospects. The proposed approach is evaluated on various datasets and compared to alternative important component selection methods. By focusing on vital brain regions and connections, we demonstrated that rs-fMRI data can be distilled into a more concise, yet informative representation that enhances ADHD classification using Deep Learning models, resulting in improved diagnostic accuracy and simplified model complexity. Furthermore, the selected essential components showed a significant correlation with established ADHD criteria, as validated by the STING toolbox. Our findings outperformed previous studies and surpassed the performance of widely employed complex Deep Learning models, highlighting the method's efficacy in rFMRImalization. The proposed method can be applied to other complex classification tasks and has far-reaching implications for effectively utilizing high-dimensional rs-fMRI data in machine learning models. To address this issue, the Acronym Disambigation Game was created, allowing multiple stakeholders to contribute to the resolution of this problem. Our system, MadDog, is a comprehensive web-based platform that supports acronym discovery, identification, and disambiguation, incorporating a search engine and interactive interface for groups of human annotators. MadeDog is further enhanced with advanced data processing capabilities and a user-friendly interface for data retrieval, enabling the reuse of annotated data for training machine learning models or directly applying human-generated annotations to target texts. MadDog is accessible at [www.maddog.io](http://www.maddog.io). A detailed demonstration of its functionality is available online at [this link](http://maddog.io/demo). Instructions for utilizing the system, including data preparation guidelines, are available at [these instructions](http://maddog.io/docs). Quantum interference plays a significant role in shaping the flow of electric current and heat in quantum Hall systems, particularly at junctions where different Landau levels are involved.  This feature can be leveraged to conduct heat within these systems and even serve as a mechanism for achieving exceptional thermoelectric properties.  In this study, we examine the effects of quantum interference on electric current and heat in quantum Hall junctions involving two and three terminals, analyzing conditions under which interference induces significant heat buildup within the junction.  This heat generation can be made more efficient through the implementation of a quantum interference wedge structure, which increases the absolute value of the thermoelectric figure-of-merit in this system, even reaching a perfect value under specific conditions.  Furthermore, we demonstrate that this concept can be used to develop an on-off thermoelectric system in which a thermoelectric current is directed only when a certain lead is connected.  This novel mode of thermoelectric functionality has potential applications in a variety of fields, including the development of highly efficient heat conductors and pumps.  In addition to these properties, we have also investigated heat rectification in quantum Hall junctions with varying levels of resistance connectivity.  Our results show that heat rectification can occur under a wide range of circumstances, with the effect often influenced by interference; in particular, we have found that a specific type of wedge structure can serve as an exceptionally effective heat rectifier.  This research provides fundamental insights into the behavior of electric current and heat within complex quantum Hall systems, potentially enabling the development of innovative, high-performance thermoelectric devices.  In the associated resources, we provide step-by-step instructions on how to implement the numerical methods used in this study, as well as the full source code for these simulations.  Additionally, we have included a guide on how to construct the specific type of wedge structure found to exhibit exceptional heat rectification properties.  This information may be useful to readers for either verifying the results presented in this study or developing their own innovative versions of the described numerical schemes and physical mechanisms. By controlling the value of $k$, we can optimize the size of each node, which enables efficient data compression and, therefore, a larger storage capacity. The choice of $n$ determines the depth of the tree, which affects retrieval and data access speeds. Topological materials exhibit unique properties that can be linked to specific topological invariants located at specific points in space. However, a relatively recently recognized phenomenon involves topological invariants located at lines in momentum space, which are nodal lines (NLs), characterized by linear dispersion along two directions and a gap in the third. This review focuses on these NLs, discussing theoretical aspects, their topological properties, and recent realizations in photonic systems, as well as realizations in other systems, including Dirac semimetals, where they are protected by symmetry. We also examine experimental observations of NLs via ARPES and scanning tunneling microscopy, highlighting their distinct signatures and potential adaptations for experimental purposes. Lastly, this review delves into the relationship between NLs and a variety of other topological structures, before concluding with an examination of potential applications and future avenues for research. Due to the absence of extrema along the lines, NLs are difficult to probe using conventional methods, requiring sophisticated analysis to extract their characteristics. Nonetheless, recent breakthroughs have enabled the study of NLs using various techniques, unlocking their potential for applications in valleytronics, spintronics, and the manipulation of light. As such, this topic is poised to contribute significantly to the advancement of photonic and other topological systems, making it an exciting area of research to explore further. We suggest developing innovative methods not only to study NLs but also to create topological structures with complex connections, such as topological flat ribbons, and harness their unique properties for cutting-edge technologies. This could lead to the development of ultra-broadband photonic devices, and new breakthroughs in research on topological materials, semiconductors, and other materials. Furthermore, exploring new concepts for generating NLs via magnetic field modulation of NLs in Dirac semimetals, and adapting these techniques to other systems, could yield substantial gains. Lastly, realizing artificial NLs in atomic systems via Rb-eatome gas, and examining their properties via ARPES, represent promising avenues for research and potentially opening new avenues in valleytronics. These potential advancements make the study of nodal lines a pivotal area of research to monitor the evolution of topological materials and contribute to innovative technologies. It holds great potential to enable novel applications with the potential to revolutionize the fields of photonics and spintronics. Therefore, it presents an exciting opportunity to advance our understanding of topological materials and potentially develop groundbreaking technologies. In tissues driven by an autonomous oscillator, like the intestinal epithelium, a steady wave pattern is seen throughout much of its length, despite the oscillator's periodic source of activity, which usually generates solitary waves under normal conditions. To explain this discrepancy, we present a mathematical model of the oscillator's and receiving tissue's behavior, incorporating a complex system of differential equations. By analyzing this model, we determine the conditions necessary for both solitary and stationary wave formations. Our analysis of solitary wave behavior reveals how the speed of these waves, which are incredibly fast when the oscillator is very active and slow when it is very inactive, can exhibit a sudden, extreme change in response to minor alterations in the oscillator's activity level. To address this issue, we develop an analytical method for estimating the speed of regenerative waves under various physiological conditions. Our model, which includes an analysis of the dynamics between an oscillator and a receiving tissue, provides a clear understanding of how the sudden, extreme changes in wave speed could serve as trigger mechanisms for certain cellular processes. Additionally, we explore the possibility that the model's temporal dynamics, which is driven by the oscillator alone, could contribute to the development of spatial patterns in cells. Our analysis reveals how the alternating periods of high and low activity between adjacent cells could give rise to a wide range of distances between successive wave peaks. Our model also shows that the amplitude and duration of these periodic fluctuations can be accurately estimated using our analytical speed formulas. Furthermore, we find that the cell-to-cell distance, which is influenced by the oscillatory mechanism, can also be accurately estimated using our analytical speed formulas. To validate our approach, we use our results to explain a previously reported phenomenon in which the length of intestinal crypts increases following the elimination of primary oscillator cells at their base. Our analysis reveals how this phenomenon can be attributed to a significant shortening of the wavelength of waves generated by the remaining oscillator cells at their new trigger zones. Our approach provides a new understanding of the underlying mechanisms that control the length of cellular patterns due to the loss of autonomous oscillators. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our model, which is based on the analytical speed formulas, can successfully reproduce the observed decrease in cellular pattern length. Our approach thus offers a valuable tool for predicting and clarifying the spatial and temporal dynamics of cellular systems driven by autonomous oscillators. We have developed two entropy estimation protocols utilizing quantum subsystems with limited dimensions. The first, based on entanglement into a qubit, allows for estimating von Neumann entropy with a worst-case error of $\varepsilon$ using $O(\frac{\log^2 N}{\varepsilon^2} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ subsystems. The second, involving entanglement into a qutrit, achieves a similar error with $O(\frac{\log^3 N}{\varepsilon^3} + \frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ subsystems. Both methods can also accurately estimate specific measures related to multiplicative divergence and mutual information, respectively, with similar resource estimates. The developed protocols offer advantages in terms of resource usage over previously known classical methods. The estimated resources are also shown to be nearly optimal for entropy estimation, within a constant factor, for both protocols. The analysis includes a detailed study of minimization problems in information theory. The developed protocols are likely to be valuable in quantum computing and related experiments for quantifying randomness in quantum states. The results were recently extended to estimating conditional entropy and other information-theoretic quantities in a related arXiv paper. The proof of a key lemma's optimality was later streamlined in a related arXiv paper. The research was recently developed into a letter in Nature Communications, providing more accessible explanation and outlining the practical implications of the findings. The results were further presented at the 2022 IEEE Information Theory Society's Bob Adamyan Memorial Workshop on Information Sciences. The findings were also discussed at the 2022 Quantum Information and Computing Symposium. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/quantum-estimation-and-control/entropic-qmc. In clinical settings, coding medical data accurately according to the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is crucial for research, policy development, and public health initiatives. Current methods for accurate coding rely heavily on experienced medical coders, who undergo extensive training and yet often fail to achieve perfect results. To improve and streamline coding, we propose a semi-self-supervised approach combining pre-trained transformer language models with autoencoding and adversarial training techniques. By adapting these methods to the ICD coding task, we can significantly reduce the need for manual labeling during the supervised training process, utilizing existing coded data more efficiently. Evaluation results on a large US healthcare dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our semi-self-supervised model in producing accurate ICD codes with minimal labeled data, outperforming existing state-of-the-art baselines consistently. The proposed model's source code is available publicly at https://github.com/health-arts/ICD-CodeGenerator. Our model's results have been validated through rigorous evaluation on multiple healthcare applications, demonstrating improved performance, faster training times, and enhanced generalizability across diverse clinical scenarios. Specifically, our model achieves superior performance with minimal labeled data in tasks such as clinical event extraction, patient re-identification, and retrieval-based on ICD codes. With its high efficiency and accuracy, this semi-self-supervised approach holds great promise for the efficient handling of large medical datasets and various healthcare applications. This paper explores the length of the Rees algebra of $R$ with respect to the monomial ideal $I$, denoted as $\mathbb{Z}_k\ast R/I$. Specifically, we examine the extent to which the Cohen-Macaulay property in the Rees algebra of $R$ with respect to $I$ applies to ideals $I$ that are nearly Cohen-Macaulay, given that this class includes linear and polymatroidal ideals. Additionally, we provide specific criteria based on the Krull dimension of the saturation of $I$ and offer illustrative examples. Furthermore, we investigate the extent to which the nearly Cohen-Macaulay property in the Rees algebra is invariant under specific transformations of the ideal $I$. Specifically, we look at its behavior under taking upper or lower linear components and its relation to polymatroidal ideals. Lastly, we investigate the Hillum-Bourain's conjecture for polymatroidal ideals. Specifically, we demonstrate that these ideals exhibit the required property for $q=2$, thus verifying the conjecture for this case. However, we also present counter-examples that show the conjecture does not apply generally to polymatroidal ideals. Rather, we identify a more general condition based on the primary decomposition of the ideal $I$. Finally, we propose an open question related to the behavior of the length of the Rees algebra for polymatroidal ideals when the base field is changed. Specifically, we consider whether this length remains constant or can be expressed as a linear function of the base field characteristic $p$. We provide supporting numerical data and examples for our inquiry. Furthermore, we offer a conjecture that the length of the Rees algebra for polymatroidal ideals is a polynomial function of the base field characteristic $p$. Specifically, we propose the degree of this polynomial to be $p-1$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this degree is at least $p-1$ and present numerical data and examples as evidence. Finally, we conjecture that the polynomial function of the base field characteristic $p$ describing the length of the Rees algebra for polymatroidal ideals is actually monic and positive. Researchers have made significant progress in incorporating variational algorithms, such as Bayesian neural networks, into quantum hardware. However, current quantum Bayesian learning methods are limited in that they require large numbers of shots to function reliably. We have developed a new, noise-reduced approach called Variational Unsupervised Bayesian Embedding, which effectively trains on data from a quantum circuit without requiring numerous measurements. Our method combines principles from quantum phase estimation and the Lanczos algorithm to achieve this goal. By combining this technique with a new technique called Guided Learning, we have successfully trained a Bayesian neural network on just three data points, accurately reconstructing a quantum circuit's output with high fidelity. Our methods are versatile and can be applied to a range of functions, as well as to classical datasets. Furthermore, these techniques can be extended to train quantum circuits that surpass the No-Cloning theorem, a fundamental quantum principle. With further advancements, quantum circuits may be able to learn beyond what is possible classically. The techniques described here are currently available on Qiskit. Differentiable rendering has emerged as a highly effective tool for solving inverse problems in computer vision, particularly those involving 3D scenes. However, traditional methods relying on ray marching or tree-based rendering algorithms are too slow for use in gradient-based optimization techniques. In response, researchers have developed faster, unbiased rendering methods, yet they often neglect critical factors like surface normals, texture, and lighting, which significantly impact the accuracy of reconstructed 3D shapes. This paper introduces an accelerated and differentiable rendering pipeline, incorporating a new, fast shadow computation approach that considers surface orientation, texture, and environment map information. Our model, called SMM-Marshaller, includes a novel memory structure that efficiently stores and manages large surfaces, enabling precise shadow generation without inverting the rendering model. Our method outperforms current standards in both accuracy and speed, with a significant improvement of up to 10x faster, while achieving superior reconstructions with up to 10% improved SSIM. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the validity and generalizability of our approach, validating its potential for a wide range of applications. Our code will be publicly available on GitHub.

Recent advancements in intelligent transportation systems (ITS) technology have made it possible to gather a considerable amount of data on the dynamics of transportation networks. This data includes information on how demand for specific routes changes over time, which can be used to develop models that learn from data and make accurate predictions. One approach in this study involves creating a framework for using large datasets of transportation records to estimate the probability distribution of origin-destination demands. This is done by developing an iterative procedure that utilizes empirical Bayes methods and makes no assumptions about the shape of the distribution. Results show that as the dataset size increases, the estimated probability distribution becomes more accurate and concentrated around the true values. Additionally, the effects of dataset size on estimation accuracy are quantified through statistical analysis. This study provides a basis for further research on developing transportation models that can learn from data in the future. This paper introduces the MusicTM-Dataset, a comprehensive collection of multimodal music information. It encompasses three-dimensional datasets comprising sheet music, song lyrics, and corresponding audio, all aligned, covering a range of 100 songs in the classical genre. The MusicTM-Dataset is designed to facilitate the development of unified representations for these three modalities, enabling more effective multimodal learning and applications. The dataset can be utilized to learn modalities individually or in combination; we provide preliminary results of such learning experiments in this study. Additionally, it offers opportunities for multimodal pre-training and fine-tuning for a variety of tasks, including music classification, transcription, and generation. To maximize its utility, we have made the MusicTM-Dataset publicly available for research at https://github.com/jaychung7/MusicTM-Dataset. It is intended to be expanded with more diverse content, including songs from other musical styles and styles from non-Western cultures. Our aim is for the MusicTM-Dataset to become a standard reference for research in multimodal music domain adaptation and translation. We've analyzed the behavior of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation in optical systems with respect to solitons and dark solitons under the influence of intensity-dependent dispersion. Our research reveals that, in contrast to solitons, dark solitons demonstrate a unique property: they are susceptible to an increased effective refractive index resulting from intensity-dependent dispersion, which in turn amplifies their transverse instability. Moreover, we have obtained and examined experimentally-derived thresholds for the dark-solon radius and finding that the increased effective index surpasses the soliton's index only when the dark-solon radius exceeds a certain value. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that the increased effective index can initiate an explosive explosion of radiation in the far field following a small initial disturbance to the dark soliton, and we have numerically calculated the emitted pulse duration as a function of the dark-solon radius. Consequently, we have concluded that optical systems with intensity-dependent dispersion will destabilize dark solitons but will actually stabilize solitons. Interestingly, this peculiar property of dark solitons may offer a novel mechanism for generating short pulses of light. A generalized approach has been developed to optimize stellarator coil designs for various magnetic configurations through a unified framework. The coil enhancement method, initially proposed by S. S. Nosenko, is expanded and formalized here. The core idea involves identifying and removing magnetic discontinuities, which are generated by the differential of an optimal gradient in a reference magnetic configuration. This method is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of stellarators, as demonstrated by optimizing coil designs for the NCSX experiment using three distinct iterative integrable coil optimization methods and three distinct reference magnetic configurations. The enhanced coil designs successfully eliminate all first-order magnetic discontinuities, achieving a remarkable 99.97% efficiency across all cases. Furthermore, these coil designs exhibit exceptional robustness, with minimal variations in their structure when transformed into quasi-Tokamak configurations. The enhanced coil designs also demonstrate an impressive level of symmetry, as evidenced by their low geometric global indices. The stellarator's modular structure is reflected in its geometric global invariants, with each module displaying a comparable level of coherence. The exceptional structural properties of these coil designs directly contribute to their remarkable efficiency and robustness. The generalized approach developed here can be applied to the optimization of various stellarator designs and can serve as a valuable assessment tool to evaluate the quality of different coil designs. The method's general framework and concepts can also be used to study and characterize the underlying structure of stellarators. The full documentation of the code used to generate and analyze the enhanced coil designs is publicly available at https://github.com/CompPhysEU/NCSX-Coils/blob/master/Documentation/Coil_Evaluation_Documentation.pdf. The public database of enhanced coil designs, including all results, can be accessed at https://github.com/CompPhysEU/Coils_DB. The database includes stellarator optimization results for NCSX using three reference configurations and three coil optimization methods, with a wide range of geometric topologies and various stellarator design characteristics. The enhanced coil designs were optimized using three distinct iterative integrable coil optimization methods: the reference coil method, the planar coil method, and the quasi-toroidal coil method. The full documentation of these algorithms and the public database of enhanced coil designs can be accessed at https://github.com/CompPhysEU/NCSX-Coils/blob/master/Documentation/Coil_Evaluation_Documentation.pdf. The public database includes all results for the stellarator design characterized by a general K-diagonal symmetry with 8 quadrupole magnetic field points and a strong field aspect

A detailed thermal analysis of a gas-solid fixed bed is carried out using a novel approach that combines computational heat transfer with experimental temperature measurements. The experimental method employs rapid magnetic resonance imaging to determine temperature distribution in real-time, accurately representing the complex heat transfer conditions observed in the experiment. The agreement between experimental and computational results validates the numerical model, enabling the identification of key heat transfer processes occurring at specific scales within the bed. The study finds that the correlation between temperature and particle velocity is influenced by the relative importance of convective and radiative heat transfer on a per-wake basis. The existence of a stable temperature non-uniform pattern is confirmed, and the effect of bed voidage on the temperature arrangement is investigated. The relationship between temperature non-uniformity and the average bed voidage is established, and the impact of global flow rate on the temperature arrangement is explored. The experimental and computational results are comparable, revealing how varying flow rates and bed voidages affect the in-bed temperature distribution. The study provides new insights into the in-bed temperature non-uniformity and offers a framework for understanding its origin, extent, and sensitivity to external conditions. The research has significant implications for industrial applications, and the findings may contribute to a deeper comprehension of the underlying physics, ultimately enabling the control of in-bed temperature non-uniformity. The study offers a framework for seamlessly integrating correlation functions into numerical models, and the results can guide the development of more accurate numerical models, enhancing the precision of computational models and predictive models based on machine learning. The research provides a universal understanding, and the findings can be translated to other domains, and the work can contribute to advancing the field through more accurate computational models and predictive models, and the integration of correlation functions into numerical models. The study offers novel insights and demonstrates the capabilities of combining advanced imaging techniques and numerical models for an in-depth understanding of complex phenomena in fixed beds. A generalized framework, applicable to any number of components, outlines a criterion for spontaneous aggregation formation and identifies all possible configurations through a mathematical representation. Furthermore, the theory reveals the existence of unique aggregates, theoretically predicted to be stable within any partitioning of the system's volume. These predictions are confirmed in contact with an infinite reservoir of each monomer species, and the theory is applied to systems involving four or more different components. The outcomes are compared to earlier results obtained for three-component systems, highlighting their similarities and differences, and the implications are discussed in terms of cell biology and the formation of cellular structures. Finally, the framework's limitations and potential extensions are examined. Specifically, the theory's applicability is extended to systems involving polymers of the same type through the application of different mathematical representations. However, the theory is found to be insufficient for describing the behavior of polymers of the same species, and the possibility of applying the theory to systems involving a single type of polymer is explored. Certain unique aggregates, previously identified, are found to be stable in systems involving a single type of polymer, and their characteristics are discussed in terms of their applicability to cellular biology and the construction of cellular structures. Finally, the possibilities are opened up for a broader understanding of cellular biology and the development of general methodologies for designing artificial cellular structures. Possible experimental methods for confirming these predictions are also explored. These predictions could be confirmed through the application of fluorescence microscopy or other labeling techniques applied in contact with an infinite reservoir of each monomer species. The comparison of theoretical and experimental results could provide a deeper understanding of the spontaneous formation of cellular structures and ultimately contribute to the development of novel methods for designing self-assembling materials. These materials could potentially be used for a broad range of applications, and the general methodologies for designing artificial cellular structures could one day be utilized in fields such as medicine, where novel treatments could be developed using self-assembling materials with specific properties. These materials could be designed to target specific cells or tissues. Similarly, novel materials could be developed with specific properties and designed to target specific diseases. Ultimately, the development of novel materials could one day be utilized in the construction of novel therapies. These could take many forms, from novel cancer treatments that could one day be developed using self-assembling materials capable of targeting and destroying specific cells, to novel gene therapy techniques that could one day be utilized using self-assembling materials capable of targeting and modifying specific DNA sequences. These are just a few examples of the many novel materials could one day be utilized in the construction of novel therapies.

Several key properties are showcased, such as simple homotopy equivalence, Poincaré duality, and Madsen-Weiss theorem compliance. Additionally, the criterion is applied to yield an alternative proof of the Mumford Conjecture for complex curves by building on the relationship between topological properties and the geometry of algebraic surfaces. The integration of stable homotopy theory via the b-principle also offers a framework for a general approach to geometric Poincaré duality. A key concept in achieving this proof involves the construction of a topological structure that can be projected onto a surface containing a specified simple topological feature in a way that preserves the underlying geometry. Several general strategies for constructing such projections in various dimensions have been developed and will be discussed, along with their applications across multiple cases. A crucial technique employed in these constructions is b-principle-induced decomposition of topological structures, which often relies on the use of nilpotent spaces and their properties of vanishing higher homotopy groups. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of the methods used by these researchers, focusing on the algorithms and strategies employed for solving cardiac mechanics problems. The aim is to offer transparent and modifiable code to the community for conducting similar analyses and contributing to the development of efficient solution methods. Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of comprehensive algorithmic documentation and the potential of interdisciplinary collaboration in advancing the development of efficient solution methods. These techniques can be applied not only to cardiac mechanics but also to a wide range of other complex physical simulations. Ultimately, the solutions and insights gained from this research can be adapted to tackle other complex problems in fluid dynamics and flow physics. In this study, we conduct an extensive examination of how various methods of setting hyperparameters for evolutionary algorithms (EAs) affects their overall performance. To achieve this, we employ three different techniques for global sensitivity analysis to compare the impact of different hyperparameter configurations on the performance of EAs in solving a diverse set of optimization problems, as defined by the CEC2017 benchmark suite. The findings from our analysis indicate that the suitability of different hyperparameter configurations is problem-dependent, with no single method outperforming others across all optimization problems studied. However, our results do suggest that the volume of suitable parameter space for each EA is significantly reduced when using sampling-based hyperparameter optimization compared to adaptive programming methods, and that the performance of EAs is largely insensitive to minor variations in suitable hyperparameter values. The insights gained from our study can inform the development of more robust sampling-based hyperparameter optimization methods, while also providing a theoretical basis for justifying the use of adaptive programming methods in specific optimization domains. The analytical framework developed in this research can be employed to investigate the sensitivity of EA performance in a wide range of optimization domains using various global sensitivity analysis methods. Furthermore, our study provides a quantitative assessment of the relative effectiveness of different hyperparameter configurations, which can be utilized to develop more accurate models of suitable parameter spaces and inform the development of novel sampling-based hyperparameter optimization algorithms. The interpretation of quantum wave functions remains unclear, with different methods producing distinct pictures of a particle's location. I argue that the spherical wave formula, commonly used in perturbation theory, offers a superior representation of a particle's state. This is because it incorporates the particle's total energy, ensuring that long-range perturbations have a significant impact on the wave function, a condition met in many practical situations. I demonstrate the necessity of including long-range perturbations in the context of scattering, using the example of a particle interacting with a weak, spherical potential that decreases with distance. The spherical wave formula's conditions are more naturally satisfied by problems with spherical symmetry, a case study involving the hydrogen atom will be discussed in further detail. Recent breakthroughs in reinforcement learning have been largely facilitated by specialized environments, such as Atari games and robotic tasks, which have driven advances in both algorithms and experiments. However, a significant gap remains in evaluating the overall effectiveness of reinforcement learning training across diverse tasks. To address this challenge, we introduce L2E, a unified framework that encompasses a comprehensive suite of evolving learning scenarios, which simulates a real-world academic setting. L2E is comprised of multiple modules: a task generator, an experiment scheduler, and a robust evaluation algorithm that assesses the training process objectively. We utilize synthetic environments to demonstrate the functionality of L2E and carry out a comprehensive study to examine the impact of varying hyperparameters. Furthermore, we provide open access to L2E, a Python package available on GitHub, which enables the community to contribute, replicate results, and utilize L2E in future research and development endeavors. We anticipate L2E to play a pivotal role in fostering collaboration and innovation in reinforcement learning. The source code is available at https://github.com/learn2evaluate/l2e. This study explores a novel type of solution to the 2D Euler equation, where the velocity field and surface elevation of waves are both smooth and vary smoothly with time, but unlike traditional wave behavior, they don't follow the standard Euler equation dynamics near a Couette flow boundary. Instead, as the distance from the boundary decreases, the solutions behave erratically, defying certain efficient algorithms and singularities that normally occur in similar scenarios. Furthermore, as the distance from the boundary increases, the solutions revert to standard Euler equation dynamics, restoring stability and the possibility of analytical calculations that were previously available. Notably, these new solutions exhibit chaotic behavior, like the type seen in the Kolmogorov flow, but this behavior is confined to a narrow, bounded area near the Couette flow boundary. This research also confirms the existence of singularities under specific conditions, validating previous conjectures regarding the nature of these new solutions and the underlying geometry of the problem. Finally, at a certain Reynolds number, these new solutions exhibit a form of statistical equilibrium, akin to the Alexeev limit cycle, and can be accurately modeled using a unique type of solution to the 2D Euler equation. Additionally, we demonstrate the ability to create dual-component condensates with controlled polarization, demonstrating the optical manipulation of separate polariton condensates through a method akin to optical tweezers. These findings enable new avenues for optical control over polariton condensates, influencing their subsequent emission. Furthermore, this technique holds potential for applications in spin-based information technology and quantum computing. Lastly, our research also offers an innovative method for creating vortex states within polariton condensates. This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproofs for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) type equations that incorporate nonlocal "slope" terms. A specific nonlocal equation was introduced by Berestycki, Loges, and Stone in 2019 as part of a broader class of fractional KPZ equations. We examine the well-posedness of this specific equation and its variants under distinct nonlocal conditions within a broad class of deterministic KPZ type equations introduced recently by Hamel and Aroua. Our main findings demonstrate that the introduction of nonlocal "slope" terms leads to unique properties in these types of equations, particularly regarding their solutions' uniqueness and continuity with initial data. These results contradict some previously held conjectures about the fractional KPZ equation's behavior. Additionally, our study's approach contributes a novel technique for addressing fractional KPZ equations' well-posedness, which may be applicable to other related problems in the field. A key variation of our main result has far-reaching implications, connecting the fractional and state-dependent KPZ equations in a meaningful way. Specifically, our result implies that the solutions to the state-dependent KPZ equation exhibit a certain smoothness when compared to their fractional counterparts, particularly under certain assumptions regarding the equation's coefficients and a fractional "commutator" quantity. This implication significantly expands upon recent breakthroughs in the field and offers a novel link between these two types of equations. Finally, our study also provides a partial answer to a previously posed conjecture by Hamel and Aroua, which suggested that solutions to a certain family of deterministic KPZ equations converge uniformly as a certain parameter, λ, approaches zero. The COVID-19 pandemic, deemed a global health crisis by the World Health Organization, underlines the significance of reliable public health data for monitoring the outbreak and making informed decisions. Governments and health authorities worldwide have to swiftly respond to evolving situations, for which having accessible and transparent data is crucial. This paper outlines the challenges South Africa faced in managing the COVID-19 crisis and proposes a data-driven approach to addressing these issues. A case study is presented, showcasing a proposed data analytics pipeline for COVID-19 surveillance. This pipeline incorporates readily available data from diverse sources, including public health platforms, transportation systems, and economic indicators, to provide real-time monitoring. A predictive analytics component enables the system to forecast cases based on historical trends. Experimental results validate the efficacy of this approach in replicating confirmed COVID-19 cases. The proposed framework serves as a public health informatics model, facilitating data-driven decision-making for the COVID-19 outbreak in South Africa and more broadly. Additionally, this system can be adapted for other countries to inform policy decisions in the ongoing pandemic. In medical contexts, extensive data sets are often characterized by redundancy, where a small subset of features holds the vital information for accurate diagnosis. This study investigates the application of principal component analysis and its variants in multimodal retinal image analysis. By evaluating different techniques on various datasets, we demonstrate the feasibility of using these methods to classify diseases, ultimately leading to diagnostic decisions. Our findings showcase the effectiveness of using these techniques on retinal images to diagnose glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy, highlighting their potential to streamline clinical processes and improve patient outcomes. This research contributes to the existing literature by conducting an in-depth comparison of these techniques and showcasing their practical utility in medical image analysis. Additionally, the code and datasets used in this study have been made publicly available to facilitate further research and development. This research has the potential to be extended to other complex diagnostic processes. X-ray images contain valuable information about lung conditions, but image quality can vary greatly in real-world settings.  Despite their potential, most studies rely on well-controlled image datasets due to difficulties in processing and predicting image quality.  This research explores the concept of potential image qualities, identifiable during hospital admissions, and investigates how they influence the accuracy of models classifying lung conditions in X-ray images.  To this end, a novel dataset of ICU indicators in X-ray images was created, and models for lung infection and severity assessment were re-evaluated with potential image qualities as additional inputs.  Our results show that knowledge of potential image qualities enhances the accuracy of models in real-world settings, and enable the identification of features and characteristics that impact image quality and model performance.  This research contributes to a deeper understanding of image quality and its practical applications in medical image analysis. This research addresses the issue of recovering a radial function on the left and right sides of a sphere given its scattering eigenvalues and properties. To solve this inverse problem, an argument based on the uniqueness of the meromorphic function is implemented, then extended to allow for piecewise constant and piecewise linear functions through the completion theorem. Ultimately, this study proves that a radial function can be accurately reconstructed from its scattering eigenvalues under mild conditions. Notably, this research overcomes a limitation in a previous study by allowing the boundary values to be arbitrary without imposing additional constraints. Additionally, this theoretical framework's implications are explored in the context of impedance transmission eigenvalues in spherically layered anisotropic media, providing a novel approach to identifying boundary conditions. Consequently, this research provides a new understanding of the relationship between transmission eigenvalues and boundary conditions, thereby shedding light on their coexistence and distinct variations. Numerical examples are also presented to demonstrate the reconstructed boundary conditions under various scenarios. This study provides a theoretical basis for using transmission eigenvalue data to analyze geophysical phenomena and materials science, facilitating the interpretation of experimental data and seismic waves that encounter layered structures. Furthermore, this research has practical implications in bioinformatics and geophysics, enriching our knowledge of how transmission eigenvalue spectra change as boundary conditions change. This research will contribute to the broad hypothesis that transmission eigenvalue spectra can discern a medium's geometry, a notion to be further tested in subsequent studies. From a mathematical standpoint, this research establishes a novel connection between completion theorems and inverse scattering problems, offering a fresh perspective on the utility of spectral theory in solving inverse problems. This study will also promote the development of spectral theory in geophysics and materials science, promoting innovative applications of spectral analysis in these fields. To expand a question-answering model's capabilities to recognize question intent, previous approaches typically relied on supervised data labeled with intent categories. However, such labeled data is often scarce in practice. To overcome this limitation, our proposed multi-stage framework tackles question intent classification in two parts: first, a series of unsupervised intent discovery processes using a pre-trained language model to identify individual intents through a contrastive learning approach, and second, refining the intent labels and aligning the question representations with the learned intents. The model's effectiveness is subsequently fine-tuned using a supervised loss function. The stages' training processes are decoupled from the existing question-answering task, allowing our approach to leverage vast amounts of unlabeled data and still deliver comparable or even improved performance on labeled data, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in question intent classification. We explore how the ABS equation's integrable properties are connected to this equation, while also reviewing conformal symmetry within this system. Furthermore, we investigate solutions to the equation, focusing on those derived using the central solution scheme along with singular solutions, including a special case of the pole-zero collision. Our analysis also reveals that the ABS equation exhibits a wealth of algebraic structure, connected to Novikov algebras, and we examine the related U-grade graded Lie algebra. We also consider the equation's extension to 3 dimensions, while looking ahead to future research avenues. Finally, we provide a brief overview of related works in the field. Our review aims to introduce readers to the key concepts underlying the ABS equation, while also showcasing the variety of novel approaches being developed to address its associated challenges. We hope that this review will inspire fresh insights into this dynamic area of research. In the realm of image understanding, the task of visual relationship detection focuses on pinpointing the connection between two key objects within a given image. Unfortunately, the accuracy of this task is frequently marred by a high rate of incorrect positive predictions. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel metric called ER-curve, which offers a clear and concise visualization of model performance in this regard. By utilizing this metric, we are able to effectively assess how well each model controls false positives. A new method known as weak measurement has gained significant attention in both theoretical and experimental fields. It allows for the measurement of a property of a system without substantially altering its state, which is in line with the principles of quantum mechanics. To achieve this, weak measurement employs a probe qubit that interacts with the system of interest. Following the interaction, the probe qubit is measured to obtain information about the system's property. From an economic perspective, the information gained can be viewed as 'price', and the objective is to determine this price. Building on previous research that quantified information as a non-negative value, this study develops the equation for quantum correlation price (QCP) and demonstrates its ability to predict outcomes for a variety of measurements. QCP serves as a crucial tool for assessing the effectiveness of weak measurement procedures. Furthermore, this research examines the relationship between QCP and the Lagrange multiplier in constrained optimization, which in this case is the constraint of unit probe density matrix. This investigation also generalizes the concept of QCP to the scenario of multiple degenerate ground states. Through thorough analysis, this study verifies the feasibility and precision of QCP as a measure of weak measurement accuracy. This trajectory represents the dynamic changes in a system's state following a weak measurement. In summary, this research provides a comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the principles and applications of weak measurement and geometric quantum mechanics. As such, it holds significant potential for advancement in both fields. At the theoretical level, this research delves into the soul of quantum mechanics by generalizing QCP for arbitrary interaction Hamiltonians. This research is further developed by incorporating novel techniques for enhancing QCP, which in turn amplifies the algorithm's precision and efficiency. Ultimately, this research presents a unified quantum algorithm for determining QCP with high precision, which is substantiated by numerical simulations using random data. Current methods for AI-powered storytelling often disregard these deeper social relationships, instead relying on superficial connections such as spatial associations. To address this limitation, we have developed a cutting-edge neural network called the Social Relationship Graph Generator (SRGG). The SRGG utilizes a person-centric approach to generate social relationship graphs that reflect the intricate dynamics between characters in a story. The accuracy of these social relationship graphs is measured by comparing them to established dictionaries of social relationships. We have thoroughly tested the SRGG on three diverse datasets: the Social XE dataset, which comprises English transcripts of conversations, the Danish Social Network dataset, and a set of Danish TV scripts. The efficacy of the SRGG was evaluated in a benchmark study that assessed its performance under three different scenarios. The results demonstrate that the SRGG consistently outperforms traditional network generation algorithms, including the Erdos-Renyi model and the configuration model, in accurately reproducing social relationship graphs that conform to established social relationship dictionaries. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the generated social relationship graphs revealed that the SRGG captures nuanced character traits and story themes. To address this issue, a new method called MCMTME is proposed, which utilizes a search-based approach to optimize MCM units and ensure they are well-matched. Secure Processing, a term that encompasses chip-level security, is the primary focus of SafeChips, a leading research area. This paper proposes the Virtual Safeguard Platform, a fully- customizable, five-stage pipelineable Secure Processor, to complement existing systems protecting data-in-transit. By integrating the Trusted Hardware Extension (THIE) library from Microsoft, we developed a functional, hardware-based Secure Processor, overhauling the classic Pipeline Processor architecture to accommodate Programmable Circular Buffers and Tail-Merging Queues. The Virtual Safeguard Platform's performance, assessed using RISC-V benchmarks, shows promising results with a negligible 8% average cycle overhead for R-type instructions, despite a minimal 0.12% increase in hardware area. This innovative approach brings Secure Processors closer to practical implementation in real-world technologies. As leading research has been done on fully-hardware vs. fully-firmware Secure Processors, this project stands out in overhauling the System-on-Chip Unit, a fundamental block in modern electronics, to address Secure Processing challenges. The rotation period of a star can be an indicator of its planetary composition, as stars that have consumed planets or experience intense internal angular momentum redistribution slow down due to contraction. Our research focuses on the rotation period of MSY Venus, revealing it to be approximately 173 days, faster than Earth. We employed theoretical models to analyze the magnetic activity of both Venuses, which show that the slower rotation of our star cannot be explained solely by internal angular momentum redistribution or planet-induced contraction. However, when considering a highly turbulent and convective interior, the models indicate a possible connection between its slow rotation and the engagement of its core in an energy generation process, or an alternative explanation of intense internal mixing that led to a star's contraction. We discuss both possibilities and their implications for the super-Earth's composition and the star's evolution. Additionally, we analyzed the H-alpha index of MSY Venus, which shows a sharp decline of about 80% compared to Earth, or about three times less active in this aspect, which is consistent with both core-driven dynamo and intense internal mixing theories. We analyzed the stellar characteristics and magnetic cycles of both Venuses, employing a widely used statistical machine learning tool, which incorporates theoretical modeling. Using the scikit-learn library, our analysis shows that the rotation period of our star cannot be accurately predicted using existing statistical models that rely on stellar surface features and magnetic cycles. However, we successfully trained a more complex model that incorporates both rotation period and H-alpha index using these techniques, which could provide valuable insights for predicting stellar characteristics in exoplanetary systems. Our research offers novel perspectives on the rotation and magnetic cycles of other stars, particularly those with exoplanets or unique internal dynamics, promoting further observation and theoretical modeling of these celestial bodies. To tackle the data sparsity problem affecting recommender systems, researchers have employed session-based recommendation (SBR) approaches. SBR models predict the next action or item based solely on historical sessions, disregarding overall user or item information. Graph neural networks have been successfully integrated into SBR systems, but existing graph construction methods rely on limited local information from the session, hindering performance. To address this, we propose an improved graph construction method that leverages both local and global session details. Notably, our proposed method combines node and graph-level features through self-supervision, effectively capturing interconnected session relationships. We also adapt co-training to refine our graph model by switching between node and graph-level labels. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed graph model, yielding superior performance in practical scenarios. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/huysy/SSGCT.untime.

The interplay between correlations and non-Hermitian effects in solid state systems is a relatively underexplored area, yet understanding this interplay is crucial for utilizing correlations to modulate non-Hermitian topological properties in solids. Our research focuses on a one-dimensional non-Hermitian topological system with fermions and an on-site interaction, examining the impact of uncorrelated and correlated systems through the mean-field approximation. The results show that uncorrelated systems maintain the topological characteristics of the non-Hermitian system, whereas correlations lead to the closure of the topological gap and the loss of non-Hermitian topological stability. The absence of exceptional points in correlated systems further highlights the distinct effects of correlations and non-Hermitian interactions on the system. The findings indicate that correlations can efficiently suppress the topological characteristics of non-Hermitian systems, paving the way for the development of correlation-assisted strategies to modulate non-Hermitian topological properties in solids. The study's outcomes provide valuable insights into the interplay between correlations and non-Hermitian effects in solid state systems and offer potential avenues for the practical control of non-Hermitian topological properties in solids through the utilization of correlations.
