Quantum tunneling between valleys in silicon has been confirmed to occur, facilitated by a valley-coherent state, which exists within the silicon crystal and connects the valleys. This coherent state enables exchange of carriers between the valleys, leading to valley interference and ultimately resulting in the swapping of valley spins. Utilizing a silicon-on-insulator platform with a buried oxide layer, we experimentally observe the valley-coherent state and the spin-swap operation, which is crucial for the implementation of quantum computing schemes based on silicon. Furthermore, we have developed an analytical model to describe the valley-coherent state and spin-swap process. Our experimental results demonstrate the presence of a relatively long-lived valley-coherent state with a decay constant of approximately 0.5 microseconds and rapid spin-swap operations, taking around 20 nanoseconds. This behavior aligns with our theoretical predictions. Additionally, we have explored the conditions necessary to maintain coherence of the valley state and have identified a range of frequencies and magnetic fields within a range of 10 kilohertz to 10 megahertz that can induce valley oscillations, ultimately enhancing the performance of quantum circuits. Our study provides the foundational understanding necessary for the practical application of silicon quantum bits. Ultimately, we aim to extend the coherence time of silicon quantum bits to a second range, surpassing current carbon-based devices and positioning silicon at the forefront of quantum computing. This work marks an important milestone in the development of large-scale quantum computers based on silicon, serving as a blueprint for the implementation of quantum computing schemes that utilize valley degrees of freedom in materials like transition metal dichalcogenides. Additionally, this research has potential applications across a broad spectrum of industries, including national security, finance, and transportation, where quantum computers can rapidly solve complex problems by harnessing the power of subtle variations in valley states. Finally, this research has also identified potential applications and implications arising from valley-based quantum effects, which may emerge in materials like silicon and are likely to influence various technologies in the near future. These potential applications and implications are particularly significant and warrant a closer examination. This work can lead to significant breakthroughs not only in the development of quantum computers but also in understanding the fundamental properties of valley states, which may lead to novel applications in the rapidly evolving world of semiconducting materials. This research has far-reaching consequences and will likely propel valley-based quantum computing a step closer to reality, paving the way for widespread adoption in industry and academia. This research has broad applications and will continue to shape the landscape of quantum computing and semiconductor research for years

This research paper focuses on developing a secure control system for a mobile robotic arm (MRA) as a leader vehicle within a multi-agent system. The MRA's control strategy must consider its complex geometry to prevent and prevent deviations, the paper argues. A novel control approach using a Control Barrier Function (CBF) is proposed to address security challenges in the MRA's movement while incorporating its unique structure. A key aspect of this approach is the introduction of a security barrier function that complements the CBH's gradient vector to prevent large-scale deviations. Simulation results confirm the efficacy of the proposed CBH and SBF methods, demonstrating better performance compared to traditional security control strategies that disregard the MRA's geometry. Furthermore, simulations to assess communication delays and external interference indicate that these security control methods remain effective. A comparison of performance among different security control strategies reveals that the CBF-based method outperforms others in tracking a straight line while minimizing deviations. Additionally, external interference and communication delays did not substantially impact the CBH-based security control method. All simulations were completed using MATLAB on a desktop computer for data visualization and analysis purposes. A practical demonstration of this security control method on an actual mobile robotic arm is planned as part of future work. The research findings suggest that incorporating the MRA's complex geometry into security control designs through a CBF-based approach offers improved performance and more realistic system representations. In the field of Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolation, the need to ensure smoothness and preserve the original shape of the data has driven the development of shape-preserving RBF interpolation schemes. This has prompted a focus on designing interpolants that not only maintain the original data points but also retain the function's derivatives. Despite advances in this area, there is a lack of shape-preserving interpolants for functions with absolute values. To address this limitation, a new family of multiquadratic RBFs is proposed, and a nonlinear interpolator is developed based on these functions. The resulting interpolator exhibits favorable properties, including absolute value preservation and monotonicity, and is accompanied by a convergence theorem. The constructability and convergence of the proposed interpolator are confirmed through numerical experiments. Furthermore, the proposed interpolator demonstrates higher accuracy and smoother results compared to existing approaches. The galactic gamma-ray pulsar domain was created by a simulation modeling the movement of pulsars, taking into account a star's formation rate, mass, and velocity, as well as various pulsar recycling mechanisms. It's based on the premise that a supernova creates a neutron star with a rotational period of about 0.1 seconds and an initial magnetic field of 10 to the power of 12 Gauss. Transportation systems are susceptible to severe disruptions from weather conditions, such as reduced visibility, slippery roads, and extreme weather, causing numerous accidents and delays. Accurate weather forecasting is crucial for the efficient operation of these systems, but this is hampered by the lack of relevant data due to the infrequent occurrence of weather-related accidents. As a result, researchers often rely on pre-classified datasets of images to train models for traffic management systems. However, these datasets are insufficient because they only recognize a limited number of weather conditions. To address this gap in knowledge, a large-scale dataset of weather-related images has been collected and made publicly available to support future research efforts. This dataset contains 112,000 images across six distinct weather categories and is the largest of its kind, spanning 24 unique sub-categories. To ensure the accuracy of classifications, a rigorous evaluation process was developed and applied to several Convolutional Neural Network models, utilizing diverse data augmentation techniques to simulate real-world conditions. This comprehensive evaluation process has enabled the development of a reliable benchmark for weather classification tasks. Furthermore, a comparison of the performance of various models across three publicly available datasets has been conducted, demonstrating the superiority of a specifically designed model on this weather-related dataset. The proposed dataset, pre-trained models, and associated code are all being made available to support future research in weather classification. This research has further contributed to the field by identifying essential image features for weather classification and by developing an innovative data augmentation approach, called the 'weather mask,' to enhance model accuracy. Additionally, a comparison of the performance of different models across six distinct weather categories has been conducted, showcasing the potential for future research in multi-class weather forecasting. Finally, an examination of the dependency between image resolution and model accuracy was conducted, revealing a notable correlation and providing valuable insights for researchers. and economic policies are influenced by ongoing social discussions about the
emergency and its consequences. By analyzing the dynamics between these norms,
we can better understand their complex relationships and prevent negative
self-reinforcing feedback loops that might exacerbate climate change. To achieve
this goal, we develop a stylized model of norm interactions, which we use to
investigate the consequences of different decision-making approaches for coping with
global warming. Our study particularly focuses on the consequences of adopting a
strict economic perspective, one that takes into account the emergency's financial
impact, and a more comprehensive approach that incorporates social and cultural
considerations. We find that the second approach leads to different outcomes than
the first one, especially in extreme cases, and that institutional decisions play a
significant role in shaping societal discussions and our understanding of the
climate's state. Our analysis highlights the importance of factoring in cultural

climate change. Additionally, our framework can be adapted to study the evolution

Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility in handling delicate objects. However, accurately modeling and controlling soft grippers remains a significant challenge, primarily due to non-linear complex dynamics and non-intuitive palm movement. To address this issue, an innovative approach integrates data-driven methods with the Koopman operator theory to create an online learning algorithm for controlling soft grippers. This novel framework allows for rapid learning and adaptation during gripper operation, effectively identifying key characteristics of soft grippers and enabling real-time feedback control. The developed control structure, informed by Koopman operator analysis, and corresponding learning algorithm were successfully tested on a multi-fingered soft gripper and demonstrated the ability to instantly learn and apply control policies for picking and grasping objects within a few iterations. This approach offers new possibilities for the rapid development and deployment of control algorithms in a variety of soft robotic applications. Experimental validation: A video can be found here: https://youtu.be/6h4b8e4kK7U Experimental setup: A multi-fingered soft gripper was used with 4 actuated fingers, controlled by a custom-made DC-DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converter) module, and equipped with several DTFT (Discrete-Time Fast Fourier Transform) sensors for detecting the grip force and identifying the object being handled. The gripper's movement was monitored using a high-speed camera, and its deformation was visually assessed during operation. The online learning algorithm was tested in a series of 20 trials, and the results were compared to existing control methods, demonstrating superior performance with the new approach. This research was partially presented at the IEEE RS2019 conference, where it received the IEEE Best Student Paper Award. One of the most fundamental and widely used techniques in machine learning is the Gradient Descent algorithm, which has numerous variants each tailored to specific problem types and structures. Despite its many adaptations, most versions of GD neglect to account for nonconvex penalties in large datasets, a characteristic of many modern data sets. Our proposed Generalized Gradient Descent algorithm addresses this limitation by developing an efficient method for handling both convex and nonconvex objectives with regularization in large datasets, a technique that draws from the Ramsay algorithm. Our work demonstrates the theoretical convergence of this method, which we then applied to the analysis of several real-world problems in high-dimensional settings, such as group sparse regression and matrix factorization. The experimental results show the merits of our method, specifically in its ability to accurately recover the true sparsity in the former example and provide competitive performance in the latter, when compared to other leading methods. We have conducted an in-depth examination of the high-redshift radio source, J2102+6015, which has an estimated age of around 145 million years. Our research includes detailed spectral analysis, precise redshift measurement, and a comprehensive physical model of the radio emission. J2102+6015 exhibits a complex spectrum with a steep negative RRR pattern and significant R and D RER emission, characteristic of younger radio sources. Our investigation of possible emission mechanisms identifies RER as the most plausible explanation. By assuming RER emission, we have developed a physical model for J2102+6015's radio spectrum, taking into account RER emission, synchrotron emission, and foreground and background point sources. This analysis allows us to estimate the RER emission zone, RER luminosity, and total RER emission luminosity, respectively. Our data indicate that J2102+6015 undergoes significant RER emission evolution, suggesting it is undergoing a significant RER emission increase. This observation supports our initial assessment of J2102+6015 as a relatively youthful radio source. Additionally, we have compiled a comprehensive redshift dataset for radio sources, including J2102+6015, to facilitate future study of the evolution of active galactic nuclei. This dataset is the most comprehensive of its kind in the z = 2-5 range, providing precise redshift measurements for sources previously estimated or uncertain. A natural language state description is a method in which real-world scenarios are described using verbal information to assist in the formation of policies in complex systems.  It presents challenges in processing language that differs from standard NLP tasks because it must incorporate the inherent uncertainty of language to inform policy-making.  This report provides a comprehensive overview of state description through natural language, covering its theoretical underpinnings, models, and applications across a variety of domains.  It also examines the practical implications and obstacles in the development of state description using natural language.  Additionally, potential future research avenues are discussed in integrating natural language state descriptions into reinforcement learning policies.  We also make available a publicly accessible webpage containing additional details and a comprehensive reference list on state description through natural language.

A novel approach to measuring cosmological parameters is proposed, leveraging deep learning to extract the Density Power Spectrum (DPS) from observed spectra of quasars, which in turn enables the estimation of the Hubble constant using the Phillips relation. By training a model on mock spectra with known DPS, we demonstrate its capability to recover the DPS in observed quasar spectra with high accuracy. Subsequently, the reconstructed DPS can serve as an input to cosmological software such as COSMOGRAM to determine cosmological parameters. This methodology has the potential to be more efficient and less expensive than current quasar spectroscopic surveys, particularly when dealing with low signal-to-noise data. Furthermore, our method can supplement and complement traditional approaches to measuring the Hubble constant and will be pivotal in the analysis of upcoming quasar spectroscopic surveys. A comprehensive description of our method, along with the associated code, is provided at https://zfdesk.github.io/ReconstructDPS/. Additionally, the reconstructed DPS and associated mock spectra are available at https://zfdesk.github.io/QuasarReconstructDPS/. Follow-up work will concentrate on the training of our model with multiple DPS models that are in consonance with different cosmological paradigms, such as Lambda-CDM, to establish a connection between DPS and cosmological parameters in a trainable model. Ultimately, this trainable model will be used to forecast the outcome of upcoming quasar spectroscopic surveys in reversing the bias induced by our current cosmological paradigm on the measurement of cosmological parameters. To accomplish this, we will employ techniques from transfer learning, feature selection, and data augmentation. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. Our goal
is to develop a basic sentiment analysis model using long short-term memory (LSTM) to see
how well it performs on these datasets. Our ultimate goal is to create a more sophisticated
model that integrates multiple sophisticated algorithms and refined datasets to achieve even
higher accuracy in predicting sentiment from a single tweet. Our findings indicate that
LSTM can achieve an average accuracy of  to be determined across our datasets, which
significantly surpasses the accuracy of the basic approach that uses individual word frequency
tables. Moreover, our research indicates that LSTM predicts sentiment with greater precision
when trained on high-quality, manually labeled datasets rather than loosely annotated ones. 
Our work on selecting the best features for sentiment prediction using recursive feature
elimination (RFE) also reveals that certain words carry considerable predictive value. 
Ultimately, our experiment validates the effectiveness of the LSTM model as a reliable tool
for sentiment analysis in the Twitter environment. The code used in this project is freely
accessible via GitHub at  https://github.com/sharabk/LSTM_TSA.Sharper.

This is because the energy released in the form of gravitational waves during the early stages of cosmic events, such as the decay of cosmic bubbles and interactions between black holes and neutrons, can lead to a permanent gravitational wave memory that lingers in the universe. This gravitational wave memory, stored in the universe's gravitational wave background, can lead to measurable effects on the spectrum of gravitational waves detected by detectors, such as LIGO and VIRGO. As a result, detecting a stable pattern in the amplitude of gravitational wave memory, stored in the universe's gravitational wave background, may enable scientists to derive valuable information about key cosmological parameters, such as the Hubble constant and the age of the universe. This insight into cosmological parameters results from analyzing the power spectrum of gravitational wave memory, a property unique to this measurement that sets it apart from standard gravitational waves. This distinction gives gravitational wave memory a unique ability to shed light on early universe phenomena, such as phase transitions and non-linear gravitational wave production processes, offering a fresh perspective on cosmology. A new approach to language learning, the "signaling game with emergent semantics," suggests that words evolve from the context of games where agents engage in a battle of "guess the meaning." To test this hypothesis, we combined a "semantic grid search" with neural and symbolic reasoning to create a language learning framework. The results show that words with complex meanings and limited semantic connections are harder to learn, consistent with the idea that words for basic objects are easier to understand. Furthermore, we found that "out of place" object representations can easily lead to misinterpretations, much like in the game. To verify our findings, we created a simple signaling game where agents learned to use object shapes as signals for spatial relationships. The output was recorded and shown to be comparable to the "signaling game with emergent semantics." The findings indicate that language learning could be seen as a form of "guess the meaning" and that words with ambiguous meanings are more challenging to learn. Additionally, we observed that misaligned object representations can result in misinterpretations, much like in the game. Lastly, we found that words with clear, unambiguous meanings are generally easier to understand. The developed framework holds promise and could be used for future studies on word meaning acquisition. The code for this project is available at https://github.com/alexanderyan-k/Signaling-Games-for-Emergent-Semantics. The data collected during this research can be accessed via this link: https://tinyurl.com/Signaling-Games-Data. The data can also be requested via email to any of the listed authors: yelab@csail.mit.edu. The data collection process is described in Section 3 of this research paper. The output and recordings from our signaling game are presented in Figure 10 and Figure 11. The output and recordings demonstrate that words with clear, unambiguous meanings are generally easier to understand, as hypothesized. Recent advances in Session-based recommendation systems have shown superior performance in addressing the difficulties posed by limited item information and fleeting user sessions. Our proposed solution, a two-stage session-based recommendation system using Candidate Rank Embeddings (CARE), addresses the item identification and ranking challenges encountered in this field. Our innovative approach enhances session modeling by incorporating item candidate information, leveraging a multi-task learning framework to jointly optimize session-based and item-level models. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the exceptional session-oriented recommendation capabilities of CARE, surpassing state-of-the-art recommendations with impressive gains of 3.06% and 10.15% in terms of overall and long-tail hit ratio, respectively. Wikipedia's collaborative framework attracts a diverse range of editors, some of whom create high-quality content with a clear educational purpose, whereas others produce lower quality content that is difficult to understand. This research aims to uncover underlying patterns in editing behavior that can be used to identify and label the content of low quality articles on Wikipedia, making it accessible to individuals who benefit from such information. By analyzing data from over 6 million Wikipedia articles and 70 million edits, our analysis reveals that specific editing patterns are consistently used to convey alternative spellings, translations, and other relevant information. Furthermore, our analysis shows that certain groups of editors consistently employ these patterns to achieve specific goals, indicating a shared strategy or approach. By identifying these patterns and the behaviors that surround them, our research enables the automatic labeling of content within Wikipedia's articles, including labels for different languages, definitions, and other relevant information. Ultimately, our findings open the door for investigating the underlying social dynamics at play in Wikipedia's editing community and how these dynamics give rise to the site's rich semantic content. From an applied perspective, our research paves the way for developing an automated system that can automatically annotate and make Wikipedia's semantic content accessible to search engines and other platforms. Our experiments show that, using the identified patterns, we can accurately identify and label articles that are part of STEM fields with over 80% accuracy, as well as detect the presence of semantically rich content in Wikipedia's articles. Our code and data are publicly available for other researchers to build upon our findings and explore in greater detail the complex social dynamics at play in Wikipedia's collaborative framework. At the same time, our results illustrate the benefits that can arise from analyzing and making sense of large datasets in the field of semantic information, revealing a promising future for data-driven applications in this domain. In machine learning, decision-based testing is gaining prominence due to its label-saving properties, allowing tests to be defined as input-output scenarios without requiring labeled data. However, decision-based models face a significant obstacle - the absence of a straightforward method to assess their behavior. To tackle this challenge, we developed a novel method to evaluate and compare the performance of decision-based black-box models in a zero-knowledge setting. Our approach leverages a white-box model from a similar classification task to derive a decision-based model's accuracy, relying only on input-output scenarios and not on actual labels or knowledge transfer. To demonstrate the efficacy of our method, we created a simplified decision-based model of a well-known binary classifier (Logistic Regression) and successfully proved that a strong model can achieve high accuracy in a zero-knowledge setting. Furthermore, our approach enables accurate classification in scenarios involving minor perturbations (adversarial attacks) and can serve as a reliable diagnostic tool to identify decision-based models with compromised functionality. Our method has been made available on our website. Additionally, the code used in this research is openly accessible on GitHub. However, expert demonstrations are often costly to obtain in complex scenarios. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new method, Co-Imitation Training (CIT), which leverages peer agents' behaviors without requiring expert input. We modify the traditional imitation learning framework by incorporating an additional agent that competes against the learner. Both agents' policies are then trained simultaneously to replicate the better-performing peer's actions. We demonstrate the efficacy of CIT through experiments in multiple settings, including peer imitation and human-agent interaction. EIL essentially acts as a supportive agent that guides the learner using more effective strategies, thereby facilitating faster agency convergence. This paper proposes a metric function that determines code correctness, along with an efficient method for calculating the minimum distance of convolutional codes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this metric function by directly calculating the minimum decoding error of parallel-convolutional codes (PCCs), also known as parallel-convolced codes (PCCs), under a binary erasure channel. The proposed metric function facilitates the calculation of error probabilities for PCCs, thus enabling the direct determination of the minimum bit-error rate in binary phase-shift keying receivers. Furthermore, we outline a step-by-step protocol to calculate the minimum decoding error of serially-convolced PCCs, and we provide numerical examples to verify our findings. Additionally, we define Perfect-Adjacent-Convergence (PAC) codes, along with a method for calculating the minimum decoding error of PAC codes. We also examine the upper and lower bounds of the minimum decoding error of PAC codes, along with some exemplary applications. Lastly, we have found that PAC codes can be used as a reliable substitute for the traditional binary erasure code in practice. In other words, PAC codes can be employed to enhance the data transmission quality over binary erasure channels. Consequently, PAC codes can also be employed as binary erasure codes. The proposed metric function offers a novel approach to studying convolutional codes, providing valuable insights that can be further expanded to higher-dimensional systems, including quantum convolutional codes, which are essential for developing quantum computing circuits with minimal errors, as required by the quantum computing industry. The metric function we have developed is analogous to the perfect-adjacent-convergence (PAC) code concept, which is reminiscent of similar techniques employed in the construction of quantum maximally-entangled-states, as commonly used in quantum computing circuits. The metric function and results presented here can be generalized to higher-dimensional systems (n > 2), enabling the calculation of minimal error rates in binary phase-shift keying receivers, along with the direct determination of minimal bit-error rates. Furthermore, the results presented here can be employed (a) to develop methods for constructing minimally-error quantum computing circuits, (b) to enhance the performance of binary phase-shift keying receivers, and (c) to develop methods for calculating minimal error rates in binary phase-shift keying receivers. The proposed metric function has been successfully tested and verified with numerical examples, demonstrating its potential to be a valuable tool in developing methods for constructing minimally-error quantum computing circuits and enhancing the performance of binary phase-shift keying receivers. Advanced robots require the ability to understand human behavior, which is driven by the interpretation of complex gestures. However, robots can only learn from predefined gestures that involve highly specific movements, limiting their understanding to common actions like waving or throwing. We have discovered that capturing the detailed interactions between human hands and objects is essential for grasping human behavior. Our research involves developing a novel, interactive algorithm to reconstruct 3D hand-object poses from real-world video sequences. The proposed method uses a probabilistic model to track each hand and its effect on the environment, then uses an optimization technique to place the hand in the observed pose. The algorithm is tested on a extensive dataset consisting of thousands of poses in everyday scenarios, as well as a smaller set of more precise movements, and is compared favorably to existing methods. Our research demonstrates that a single robotic system can learn to recognize a wide range of gestures by observing how hands and objects interact, and suggests a new direction for robotic learning. Building upon this, we provide conditions under which certain $Q$-orthogonality products can be equidistributed, where $Q$ is a Laurent polynomial. We derive new consequences of this product equidistribution, including a generalization of Weyl's equidistribution theorem for $F_\sigma$ sets, along with a quasirationality criterion involving the Bragg-Green formula, which generalizes an earlier finding by Serra, Teles, and Velan. Additionally, we apply our results to examine the behavior of certain counting functions related to the minimal exponents of $F_\sigma$ sets and show that their fluctuations are characterized by a specific pattern, thus establishing a link between our work and a broader family of classical problems in diophantine approximation. Finally, in a separate section, we investigate the unique $Q$-orthogonality products that correspond to the algebraic degeneracy points $\theta$ and show that the sets of such $\theta$ values, where a particular measure either converges to $0$ or $\mu(s)=1$, exhibit a complex topology, along with a notable property that the sequence of measures $\mu(s)$ converges to a point that varies continuously with the polynomial $Q$. This finding provides a generalization of a prior outcome by Serra, Teles, and Velan. Lastly, we present an application of our work that establishes a new pattern in the behavior of certain $F_\sigma$ set growth rates, along with a statement of broad convergence, thereby extending a prior outcome by Bajnok and Szabó. The traditional connection between spin and statistics, established by Fierz, relies on an outdated framework. By revisiting the principles of non-relativistic quantum mechanics from a more contemporary perspective, we establish a new, rigorously based connection between spin and statistics. Specifically, we show that the parity of a particle's wavefunction serves as the fundamental basis for determining its associated statistic, where an even parity corresponds to bosons and an odd parity corresponds to fermions. This breakthrough offers a simplified method for identifying the statistic of any particle, circumventing the need for complex mathematical transformations and relativistic constraints. Furthermore, our approach provides a clear understanding of the reasons behind the bosonic and fermionic nature of key particles, such as the photon and de Broglie angle particle. By integrating the principles of non-relativistic quantum mechanics and quantum electrodynamics, we derive a parity-based formula for determining the statistic of any charged particle, without requiring sophisticated mathematical manipulations. Additionally, we theoretically devise an experiment to verify the statistic of a specific particle, the de Broglie angle particle, which has a unique non-relativistic energy-momentum relationship. Finally, in an effort to promote research in this area, we pose several open questions related to the possibilities of relativistic angle particles. These concepts not only contribute to advanced undergraduate and graduate physics courses, but also offer an accessible and introductory exploration of the principles of Fierz transformation and the spin-statistics connection. As such, they serve as valuable tools for studying the fundamental aspects of quantum theory and its applications. Systematically working through these problems can help readers develop a deep understanding of these concepts. In particular, we highlight the significance of Parity as the Basis of the Non-Relativistic Spin-Statistics Connection as a valuable addition to the broader quantum information field. By connecting the principles of parities in quantum mechanics to the principles of parities in quantum information, we open the door for a new and innovative area of research, Quantum Information with Bases. A cooperative approach to modeling proposes that multiple entities work together as a team to create a unified model through coordinated efforts. On a practical level, this team consists of researchers and engineers who were able to overcome their differences by following a well-defined protocol for data exchange, ensuring that their contributions are consistent and compatible. By doing so, they can establish a joint model space and perform collaborative learning to achieve a common goal, ultimately making informed data-driven decisions as a unified team. This cooperative methodology is demonstrated through an actual application to the development of an evolutionary game dynamics model, where three experts in related fields, using different numerical techniques and data sources, work together to model an shared real-world system, and successfully train a generative adversarial model on their jointly collected data. This cooperative methodology has the potential to overcome significant technical limitations in many team-based research settings, and we therefore make our team protocol publicly available to support collaborative modeling across diverse research teams and domains. The researcher develops an analytical framework for assessing the maximum degree distribution and maximum degree-degree correlation of these codes. The study utilizes these metrics to examine how the properties of LDPC codes are impacted by the specific characteristics of this particular communication channel. The findings indicate that higher degree vertices within these codes are more likely to be associated with other vertices of similar degree, a phenomenon that becomes more pronounced as the channel's erasure probability decreases and the maximum degree of the codes increases. The researcher also discovers that this increased degree-degree correlation is a key contributor to improved error-resistance performance in the considered channel scenario. The study further explores how this correlation affects the minimum Hamming distance of the codes, revealing that it can be effectively estimated through numerical methods and experimental data when the codes' degree distributions are known. Recent studies on large language models have demonstrated in-context learning capabilities, however, the influence of diverse training corpora on these models' performance and behavior remains poorly understood.  In this research, we examine how varying the source of training data impacts the results of in-context learning with a 1.1B parameter language model.  By comparing its performance on datasets from different domains, as well as its response to similar queries across diverse datasets, we gain insight into the models' generalization patterns and in-context learning strategies.  Interestingly, our results show that the models can learn in-context both accurately and uniformly, but only when trained on corpora from similar domains, and ultimately demonstrate a maximum generalization scope of at least  14 distinct data sources.  Lastly, our study reveals the importance of pretraining data diversity for in-context learning and new task learning, prompting us to propose a new metric known as the Pretraining Data Diversity Index (PDI).  This index correlates positively with both in-context learning and new task learning outcomes in the models we have tested.  PDI could serve as a valuable criterion for evaluating and fine-tuning large language models in real-world applications. Galaxy cluster observations reveal widespread cold intracluster medium (ICM) 
that forms low-density clouds through a process of radiative cooling. However, 
numerous simulations indicate that these clouds persistently re-heat, raising 
concerns about the validity of current galaxy evolution models. We conducted a 
parametric study using high-resolution magnetohydrodynamic simulations of galaxy 
clusters to investigate the effects of radiative cooling, magnetic fields, and 
thermal conduction on the formation and destruction of cooling clouds. Our results 
demonstrate that the presence of magnetic fields strongly impacts the dynamics of 
cooling clouds, with isotropic turbulence leading to cloud fragmentation and an 
increased rate of destruction in the presence of magnetic fields. We found that 
the strength of thermal conduction has a significant influence on cloud evolution, 
with increased conduction effectively reducing the lifetime of cooling structures, 
particularly for small-scale clouds. These findings are consistent with a model in 
which magnetohydrodynamic forces continuously disrupt and re-form the ICM, 
preventing the accumulation of cooling material over long periods of time. We 
conclude that the combination of buoyant fragments and widespread small-scale 
fragments could resolve the long-standing issue of galaxy evolution models 
underestimating the lifetime of cooling structures. Furthermore, our work points 
out the necessity of high-resolution simulations that capture the dynamics of 
fragments to accurately model the cooling process. We also propose a possible 
connection between the late stages of our simulations and the formation of 
star-forming regions. We speculate that the survival of large fragments could 
potentially explain the presence of cool core peaks in the ICM even after 
dissipation of the initial fragments. On the other hand, the extensive distribution 
of small fragments could lead to an increased heat transfer and explain the 
underestimation of the lifetime of cooling structures in galaxy evolution models. 
These models may also need to incorporate the efficient heat transfer facilitated 
by magnetic fields to accurately reproduce the observed properties of the ICM 
and galaxy clusters. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the complex processes 
driving the ICM dynamics is necessary to resolve the discrepancy between galaxy 
evolution models and observations. We have prepared a set of publicly available 
movies that showcase the cooling emission and magnetic field configurations in 
our simulated galaxy clusters over a period of 1.6 Glyrs. These visual aids can 
be accessed at the following link: https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.fbum-ux63

A database of acoustic units is created and used to build a model for generating the mean spectra of unit sequences. A neural network is trained to produce the spectra of individual units, and a vocoder is used to synthesize the audio from these spectra. Evaluation of the system reveals that it produces speech with words and sentences that are recognizable in terms of overall length and spoken words, although the order of the words may vary. A major limitation is the current method's reliance on a pre-existing database of acoustic units. A more effective approach will necessitate a greater understanding of the relationship between acoustic patterns and meaningful sequences of sounds. This research focuses on developing an efficient motion planning algorithm for a robot coupled with various sensors in an uncertain environment. The problem requires minimizing a complex cost function, which involves constraints such as sensor limitations and sight range, as well as a predictive model of the target trajectory. To tackle this optimization challenge, we divide it into multiple connected sub-problems, each optimizing a specific aspect of the motion planning. This multi-stage optimization approach facilitates the use of data-driven methods to approximate complex interactions between sensors and the environment. Specifically, we employ McCormick envelope relaxation to model non-convexities resulting from these interactions, thereby enabling large-scale optimization. The proposed algorithm's performance is supported by theoretical guarantees and verified by practical experiments. The results show substantial improvements in processing speed and accuracy, with the added benefit of adaptable sensor configurations and reduced data requirements. The research demonstrates the value of data-driven McCormick envelopes in large-scale optimization applications. The developed motion planning algorithm, known as Data-Driven MMER, outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, as validated by the experimental data. Additionally, the study highlights the potential for data-driven methods to efficiently solve complex optimization problems in robotics and other robotic applications. The code for Data-Driven MMER is publicly available at the link [https://github.com/RoboDataLab/DD-MMER-CCAO]. The dataset for motion planning is publicly available at the link [https://robodatalab.github.io/DMP-Dataset/]. The sensor configurations and results are available on our lab's website at [https://robodatalab.github.io/projects/Motion Planning with Sensing Capabilities]. A central challenge in current state-of-the-art methods is the unpredictable nature of their solutions, which often diverge rapidly. To address this issue, we introduce a new control protocol that ensures stable and predictable behavior in systems with limitations. Our method is applicable to a broad range of systems, including those with non-linear characteristics and unpredictable influences. Our control approach provides clear, easily interpretable recommendations that minimize performance losses while avoiding overextension of capabilities. We evaluate the efficacy of our approach in various practical scenarios, including the management of power grids and the control of autonomous vehicles. It utilizes a fundamental model that treats the spacecraft as a binary fluid droplet under gravity and pressure forces, and identifies two opposing forces: the solar radiation pressure and gravity. When the masses of the spacecraft and Sun are in a specific ratio, a resonant phenomenon occurs, affecting its orbit and movement. The study divides these resonances into two categories: first-order and second-order resonances. First-order resonances occur when the spacecraft's rotational period aligns with the orbital periods of specific ejecta, while second-order resonances are produced by interactions between the spacecraft and pairs of ejecta. The orbital periods of these ejecta are multiplied by integers greater than one, leading to concurrent alignments and the emergence of higher-order resonances. The study also identifies and classifies various orbital periods of ejecta that can produce these resonances, and provides numerical data for specific spacecraft and Sun mass ratios. A new method is introduced for analytically determining an arbitrary electric field's influence on the one-electron Hamiltonian and subsequent overlap matrix of any tight-binding model. It's shown that this field effect can be expressed as a constant scalar multiplier applied to each atom, determining the field's interaction with the system. Utilizing this finding, the validity of a previously developed approach, individually calculating light-matter interactions in tight-binding models, is confirmed. Additionally, the approach is expanded to tight-binding models based on unit cells larger than repeating structural patterns, and it is applied to a silicon pyramidal surface to estimate the minimum required intensity for controlling a silicon dopant's behavior in an optical field. In computer vision, object recognition typically occurs at an individual part level, but a full understanding of an object requires knowledge of its entire shape. This study presents a method for obtaining a comprehensive representation of an object by utilizing key semantic points on each part to reconstruct its 3D shape. Focusing on category-level objects such as cars and airplanes, rather than specific models, we develop an optimal and resilient approach for estimating not only an object's position but also its overall shape based on the coordinates of a limited number of key points, both in 2D images and 3D scans, under varying lighting and viewing angles. By applying a general shape model to point cloud data, we are able to derive a unified representation of an object's overall shape, regardless of the original coordinate system used to collect the point cloud data. This objective representation enables a wide range of applications, including general object recognition and the creation of digital twins. By testing our approach on a large dataset of cars and airplanes, we are able to achieve highly accurate results for both their position and overall shape, outperforming alternative methods currently available. Additionally, we conduct a thorough evaluation of our method to confirm its resilience and demonstrate its robustness in a variety of challenging situations. This confirms that our approach is the most effective and resilient method for accurately perceiving category-level objects through computer vision. When dealing with the Cauchy distribution, parameter estimation presents significant challenges, primarily due to its lack of convergence in the mean. Nonetheless, researchers have developed methods to create reliable intervals for estimating its parameters, albeit these intervals do not satisfy the usual properties of confidence intervals. Notably, the intervals are finitely bounded, making them absolutely accurate, which is an uncommon feature in this context. Building on this idea, this paper proposes a novel approach to defining intervals for the Cauchy distribution's parameters, using a different framework. Specifically, we will use the variance or squared deviation as a measure of dispersion, as this quantity is finite and well-behaved. Under this alternative framework, we design intervals that not only provide precise estimates but also satisfy increasingly tight bounds as the sample size increases. These intervals are comparable to those obtained by maximum likelihood estimation and outperform them in several respects. Moreover, we examine the proposed intervals' behavior in cases of small or finite sample sizes, demonstrating that they converge rapidly and uniformly. The methods developed in this paper can also be extended to estimate the parameters of related distributions, as well as those of the within-cluster distribution in cluster-sigma models. Lastly, we illustrate the effectiveness of these proposals using numerical examples and Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have made the relevant R code publicly available at https://github.com/congdonstats/Cauchy_estimation/tree/main. This code can also be used to estimate the parameters of skew-Cauchy distributions, which generalize the Cauchy distribution and whose parameters' estimation shares similar characteristics with our proposals. A new statistical approach is needed for clinical trials that run basket trials, which assess multiple subgroups within a single trial. Traditional methods often can't accurately determine the required sample size, leading to underpowered trials. We've developed a Bayesian method for estimating sample size in basket trials that take information from all subgroups within a trial. This approach considers overall trial efficiency when calculating the required sample size for each subgroup. We've derived formulas for non-comparative basket trials and developed numerical examples to illustrate the results. Furthermore, we've simulated a scenario using Bayesian simulation to validate our findings. The results show that our method can accurately determine the required sample size, and in cases of underpowered trials, upgrading to a larger trial size significantly improves the chances of achieving the desired power. The results suggest that Bayesian methods can accurately calculate sample sizes for basket trials by borrowing information between subgroups. We've provided examples of basket trial designs that benefit from this approach, including trials assessing cancer treatments based on genetic profiles and trials using Bayesian sample size assessment to improve overall trial efficiency. Keywords: basket trials, sample size assessment, Bayesian methods, non-comparative designs, clinical trials.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput and high-precision at the system level, advanced motion control systems must be upgraded. This requires individual sub-systems, such as servomotors, to have built-in capabilities for high-precision and adaptability. Nevertheless, the traditional linear model-based control methods are not sufficiently compatible with the inherent nonlinear characteristics of motor dynamics. Furthermore, changes in the motor dynamic nonlinearity with time pose a significant obstacle to efficient model-based control strategies. This paper proposes the use of a dynamic system's dependence on time to develop a new control method for high-precision motion control systems. The proposed approach involves the creation of a sequence of linearized control strategies according to the varying system parameters' sequence. Consequently, the issue of time-varying system nonlinearity is mitigated, and the control system can effectively respond to changes in the system dynamics. This paper showcases the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy by implementing it on a state-of-the-art aeroscope platform. The aeroscope, powered by a high-precision brushless motor, demonstrates the capability to precisely move a load with a high level of accuracy even in the presence of external disturbances. The proposed control method allows the aeroscope to achieve a precision of 5 nanometers while moving at a speed of 10 millimeters per second. The success of this project has paved the way for the integration of high-precision motion control in the aeroscope, enabling the precise deposition of microdroplets on a surface in the aerospike system. A test was conducted to evaluate the precision of the aeroscope, demonstrating its capability to perform high-precision movements with a precision of 5 nanometers while moving at a speed of 10 millimeters per second. The integration of the LPV sequential loop tightening control strategy in the aerospike system allowed it to achieve a precision of 5 nanometers, meeting the precise droplet deployment requirements for the aerospike application. The code used for this research is publicly available on the GitHub repository. The model used for the LPV sequential loop tightening control is described using the Modelica language, and the simulation was conducted using the DYMICA toolset. The code for the aeroscope model, as well as the LPV sequential loop tightening controller, can be found at the following URL: https://github.com/Control-Education-Academy/2022-C5AERO21. The code used for the real-time implementation of the aeroscope controller can be found at the following URL: https://github.com/Control

We introduce a novel, self-supervised learning approach for point-to-point alignment of 3D surfaces, suited for partial object representation. Conventional alignment techniques rely on fully loaded models, whereas we focus on utilizing available, partially visible surfaces. Our method, primarily centered on learning from local, surface geometry, demonstrates exceptional flexibility and adaptability, especially in low-data scenarios. We evaluate our approach on multiple, real-world datasets, including ModelNet, UP-DM, and DP-DM, encompassing various levels of visibility and geometric complexity. Our results indicate that our method consistently surpasses existing fully-supervised techniques in point-to-point alignment. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applicability of our approach to real-world object categorization tasks. Our method is referred to as Partial Registration Network (PRNet), and the source code is available at https://github.com/your-username/PRNet.

Through this segmentation, low-level image features are leveraged to guide the synthesis of high-level cues. The effectiveness of CyDiGAN is demonstrated on two datasets, where it achieves notable performance compared to existing methods. Additionally, the resulting model showcases exceptional generalization capabilities across diverse datasets. The proposed method has been open-sourced for public access. The proposed method has been successfully applied to real-world 3D data, showcasing its effectiveness and generalizability in downstream tasks. To confirm the proposed method's efficacy, a comprehensive ablation study was conducted, with the results confirming its superiority over alternative approaches. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the method's numerical results was provided, along with a visual representation of the data, further confirming the proposed method's effectiveness and generalizability. The proposed method has been successfully integrated with a rotation-equivariant convolutional neural network (RCNN), significantly enhancing its accuracy in downstream tasks. This formulation aligns with previous constructions by Swann and Calabi. Furthermore, when considering additional structures, our approach corresponds with an elliptic cohomology theory developed by Goresky, Higson, and MacPherson. We also demonstrate that this theory is compatible with differential forms that comply with the given structures. Our analysis in this context includes a case study of the circle action on a 2-sphere with varying antipodal orientations. Temporal knowledge graph inference has emerged as a crucial application for evaluating knowledge graph embeddings (KGE). Most existing KGE models, however, assume time-invariant relationships, which fails to capture the dynamic nature of temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs). To address this limitation, we introduced a new model called Time-aware Factorized Representation (TAFR) that incorporates time-aware transformations for low-rank and model-agnostic representations. The proposed model leverages a time-dependent function for transforming vector embeddings in TKGs while being independent of any specific KGE model. Empirical results demonstrate the superiority of TAFR over high-rank and time-invariant models, and its model-agnostic property allows it to enhance the performance of existing state-of-the-art KGE models when integrated. Furthermore, TAFR's effectiveness is shown in both head-tail and tail-predication tasks for various types of knowledge graphs. To facilitate reproducibility, our implementation is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/amishah2/TAFR. TAFR's efficacy has been consistently shown in three datasets - WordNet, Freebase, and Wikidata - with a notable 5.21% relative improvement in MACE score over the strong model KGCNN when applied to these datasets. Additionally, our model exhibits a 4.69% relative boost in MACE score for head-tail prediction tasks on the WordNet dataset. To validate the model's universality, we successfully integrated it with six other strong KGE models - Tene, ComplEx, VEC, VKB, VKE, and Foulah - and observed significant improvements in inference accuracy for all these models. To further confirm the model's effectiveness in real-world applications, we evaluated it in two temporal knowledge graph inference benchmarks, where TAFR outperformed existing KGE models by achieving a 3.53% relative boost in MACE score for head-tail prediction tasks in the SNOMED CT dataset and a 2.87% relative boost in MACE score for head-tail prediction tasks in the ClinBioMed dataset. Consequently, the proposed model sets a new standard for evaluating the performance of KGE models, thereby providing a valuable tool for developers. Moreover, our model's model-agnostic property empowers knowledge graph embedding developers to enhance the performance of their models with low-rank and time-aware representations, thereby opening up new avenues for research and development. In the field of audio signal processing, the sound waves produced by vibrations in the ground due to a moving source, known as the ground effect, significantly impact measurements. Consequently, researchers face challenges when trying to pinpoint the location of sources, like explosions, by analyzing seismic data. To mitigate these issues, researchers have developed an alternative method, separate from ground effect considerations, for identifying sources in an area of interest, thus allowing them to focus on relevant information and eliminate distracting factors. To utilize this approach, the ground effect must be eliminated or removed from the data. In this research, we explore different techniques for eliminating the ground effect, such as filtering and correction, and compare their effectiveness using quantitative metrics. By applying these techniques, we are able to demonstrate the ground effect's substantial impact on seismic data but also show that it can be effectively eliminated, enabling researchers to concentrate on source-related information and make more accurate inferences. A renowned quantum phenomenon, Bell nonlocality, is examined in an ideal setting using a specific ensemble of photons. Nonlocality is typically quantified using inequalities, but this method's limitations are revealed when encountering unique correlations within a specific context. These correlations arise from a specific quantum state and emerge as non-resolving bases in a 2-dimensional space. This leads to an essential realization: the absence of Bell inequalities does not necessarily indicate the absence of Bell nonlocality. Consequently, a crucial condition is established for an ensemble to exhibit Bell nonlocality: it must yield inequalities beyond basic equality. This principle is showcased in an experimental demonstration, where an ensemble of photons in an entangled state, created through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, successfully violates an inequality despite producing equal distributions for specific measurement combinations. In modern high-performance computing, administrators must efficiently manage memory to achieve optimal system performance. A common technique for this is memory reduction by dividing the system into smaller units and evenly distributing workload across them. For a general-purpose computer architecture, a standard method is the cartridge allocation where each process or thread is isolated in its own memory segment. However, this can lead to underutilized system resources, particularly when dealing with smaller-scale applications. An alternative approach, flat partitioning, involves allocating contiguous memory segments to processes or threads, allowing for more flexible and efficient memory management. However, it is primarily used in specific applications such as network processors. Despite its potential, flat partitioning is largely unexploited in the context of general-purpose computer architecture. Our research introduces a novel run-allocating algorithm that maximizes system performance by utilizing previously underexplored flat partitioning method. This MaxFlatP algorithm can efficiently distribute workload across multiple, independently managed memory regions, even in the presence of memory fragmentation. Our experimental results demonstrate that MaxFlatP outperforms traditional cartridge allocation while offering a more adaptable solution. Furthermore, MaxFlatP rapidly finds optimal or near-optimal solutions even for complex-scale applications. In particular, it outperforms other algorithms by up to 5.46 times in finding optimal or near-optimal solutions and by up to 3.06 times in overall efficiency for a comprehensive set of benchmarks. MaxFlatP is comprised of two key components, the MaxFlatP Heuristic and Optimal Construction (HOC) algorithms and the FlatP Library (FPL). The MaxFlatP Heuristic and Optimal Construction algorithm employs a heuristic based on flat partitioning to efficiently construct and improve potential cartridge allocations. On the other hand, the FlatP Library provides a set of precomputed, high-quality flat partitioning configurations that can be easily integrated into existing operating systems to enhance their memory management capabilities. Both components facilitate efficient, high-performance system management. Our research validates the performance of MaxFlatP through extensive empirical evaluations using a custom simulator. Specifically, we analyzed the algorithm's efficiency in memory management for various applications including network processing, direct memory access, and multiple memory allocation scenarios. Our results demonstrate that MaxFlatP significantly outperforms traditional cartridge allocation in these practical tests. Furthermore, we analyzed the algorithm's parameters to identify key factors that influence its performance. Our findings suggest that cartridge size, flat partition configuration, and run allocation all contribute to the algorithm's efficiency. Our research contributes to the area by extensively evaluating the performance of MaxFlatP

We examine the openness of a background matrix of Weyl type $B$ with randomly generated entries, demonstrating that with high probability, its spectral density approaches the Weyl $B$-spectrum at a rate of $\frac{1}{\log n}$. Furthermore, this matrix's eigenvalue behavior is shown to be asymptotically independent of its diagonal entries under the spectral measure scaling, a property we utilize to study the spectral density of augmented Weyl matrices of type $B$. Additionally, the independence of eigenvalues from specific diagonal entries leads to a new, simplified approach to establishing the independence of spectral measures of distinct matrices, a concept referred to as conditional freeness, for various matrix ensembles such as GUE, GUE($\mu$), WGN, and Weyl type $B$. This method offers the advantage of bypassing the standard summation arguments over the unitary group, resulting in a more direct and conceptually intuitive proof. This approach also provides a novel, straightforward computation of the spectral measure of a matrix resulting from the entry-wise multiplication of a Weyl matrix of type $B$ by a standard normal distribution, a measure that we find to be a specific mixture of the Weyl $B$-spectrum. Finally, the openness of a background matrix of Weyl type $B$ with randomly generated entries is shown to be a necessary and sufficient condition for the spectral measures of its eigenvalue matrices to be asymptotically independent, a relationship that we refer to as conditional freeness, and this condition is also demonstrated to be equivalent to the openness of a background matrix of Weyl type $C$ with randomly generated entries under a specific spectral measure scaling. This freeness criterion, marking a significant departure from the traditional unitary group approach, is expected to play a significant role in future studies of the openness of various high-dimensional matrix ensembles. A critical comparison of our methods and approaches is made with those of recent works, including those of Chafai, Sire, and Chatterjee, with Erdos, Yuffa, and Zarfaty. This process involves an optimized image formed from eight spatial frames, which are then re-mapped into a laboratory frame to support the reconstruction of a single, optimized image. This step is crucial for facilitating the reconstruction of the gravitational field around the source object, which ultimately drives the telescope's performance. This paper presents detailed results characterizing the GRAVITY experiment's performance, which were achieved through rigorous testing of the telescope's components and associated systems. The characterization was carried out through on-sky observations and laboratory experiments, which revealed specific limitations and enabled the optimization of the telescope's performance. The telescope was then optimized for maximum efficiency and was tested in various modes, which revealed a maximum signal-to-noise ratio of about 1500. This level of performance was maintained across a wide range of spatial resolutions and the telescope was also capable of achieving a very high dynamic range of up to 6.25 in certain configurations. A common approach involves solving the vector transport equation to obtain the vorticity from the velocity's gradient. Due to the lowest-order representation of the Raviart-Thomas elements, a post-processing step, known as the patch reconstruction technique, is often applied to improve accuracy. Patch reconstruction relies on solving an extended finite element equation that involves reconstrucing the vector transport equation on mutually overlapping patches of elements. A series of numerical experiments are conducted to demonstrate the accuracy and robustness of the patch reconstruction method. The growing concern about model fairness in various industries has sparked research in equitable machine learning, particularly in the context of federated learning where data owners are sensitive to bias in learned models. Meanwhile, the increasing use of federated learning threatens data security due to the exposure of shared parameters during aggregation. To address both issues, researchers have integrated differential privacy into federated learning systems, but the protection methods often undermine fairness and privacy constraints, rendering the models less accurate. In this paper, we compile existing approaches to balancing fairness and differential privacy in federated learning, then propose two new techniques: our echo back-propagation method recasts the gradient averaging process as a weighted aggregation of local models to conceal parameter values, while our regularization-based mechanism uses implicit parameters to incur gradient noise and enforce differential privacy without compromising model fairness. Experimental results on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approaches in maintaining accurate models under differential privacy, particularly in the CIFAR-10 scenario. The source code for these techniques is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zheng-hat/FDLIP.

In this scenario, rather than transitioning to a more complex state, solutions exhibit 'feeble' behavior, resulting in a specific measure-valued solution to the corresponding boundary value problem. Introducing a new notion of 'feeble' solution, we establish the continuity of this limit and show that it is a valid solution to the original boundary value problem within a specific class of feeble solutions. These findings reveal that hadrons associated with direct photons in Au$+$Au collisions exhibit increased yields beyond expectations based on standard jet interactions. Achieving scalable quantum computing is a daunting task for both analog and digital quantum approaches. The quantum analog approach faces difficulties in maintaining coherence due to a vast number of degrees of freedom. In contrast, the digital approach using qubits can only efficiently simulate fermionic systems by doubling the dimension, which is undesirable. A hybrid digital-analog method might offer a compromise, leveraging the advantages of both techniques. By integrating the quantum analog circuit's fermionic operators with the digital qubit circuit for measurement and control, this hybrid method emulates the fermionic system's behavior. Using the Fock space representation and a numerical simulation of noise in the quantum circuit, we found that the hybrid method successfully emulates the fermionic system's dynamics while resistant to decoherence. The potential of this hybrid method to balance analog's efficiency and digital qubit's robustness makes it an attractive option for large-scale quantum computing. In machine learning, model generalizability often hinges on avoiding overfitting to complex datasets. Conventional methods typically strive for both accurate predictions and long-term performance, but inevitably compromise on one or both when faced with challenging datasets and complex models. This fundamental conflict underlies the optimization-generalization gap. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel framework centered on 'wealth functions,' which offer an explicit mathematical representation of the optimization-generalization tradeoff. By using wealth functions, researchers can proactively mitigate overfitting and improve out-of-sample performance by selectively discarding sensitive data features prior to training. Our approach is universal, applicable to a wide range of problems and models, and also offers a module-specific wealth construction method tailored for tasks involving categorical data, particularly when labels are subject to class imbalance. To facilitate practical implementation, we also develop two efficient algorithms for wealth construction. Our approach is extensively evaluated on diverse datasets, encompassing image classification, molecular kinetics prediction, and protein-ligand binding affinity estimation, often yielding superior results compared to state-of-the-art baselines and even bespoke feature-engineered models. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces a novel iterative binary-weighted fractional Hopfield neural network, which optimizes the phase distribution in a spatial light modulator to create desired structures through rapid surface reconstruction at a molecular level. The proposed system uses a binary-weighted fractional Hopfield neural network to simplify the optimization process, reducing the time it takes to converge and form multiple complex structures within a three-dimensional volume of tissues. The system achieved rapid convergence in under 3 milliseconds for forming multiple complex structures, and high fidelity with over 90% similarity for complex structures like a 3D letter within a tissue sample. The impressive performance of this iterative binary-weighted fractional Hopfield neural network-based system enables the creation of intricate structures and rapid surface reconstruction in tissues, paving the way for new applications in 3D holographic display. Advanced telescopes face significant limitations due to atmospheric distortion.  To overcome this issue, a new technique known as Fast Atmospheric Self-coherent Optics (FastASCO) has been developed.  FastASCO employs a subwavelength sample spacing phasing grid array and an artificial intelligence-assisted algorithm to identify and correct turbulence-induced speckles in a telescope's image, thereby extracting the phase structure of the atmosphere with high precision.  This technique has been successfully simulated and shown to accurately reconstruct the phase structure of the atmosphere across a wide range of conditions.  Now, for the first time, we have conducted an initial experiment using the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics (XAO) testbed to validate FastASCO's performance under real-world settings.  For a 40.64 wavelength diameter telescope, we have achieved remarkable results, including an 82% Strehl ratio and an average phase reconstruction accuracy of 76.8 milliseconds, even in severe turbulence conditions with an entire phase structure refresh rate of over 100 Hz.  These groundbreaking experimental findings confirm FastASCO's potential to provide high-quality phase structure reconstruction at extremely high speeds.  At the same time, we have discovered an unexpected benefit of FastASCO - its ability to effectively control speckles and enhance the image quality to remarkable levels, exceeding the capabilities of even advanced adaptive optics systems.  This surprising discovery has paved the way for a novel approach, fastASCO II, which integrates the benefits of FastASCO and classical AO to achieve even better results.  This new concept is expected to revolutionize the field, enabling telescopes to approach their theoretical maximum capabilities and greatly expand our understanding of the universe.  This approach could potentially enable space-based telescopes to approach their maximum potential, and even allow ground-based telescopes to approach their theoretical maximum possible limit of about 0.06 inches of image distortion, effectively eliminating the atmospheric distortion problem altogether.  This novel idea marks a significant breakthrough and will be the subject of future research studies.  This work was financially supported by the NSF grant and the DOE contract. Meta-analyses that combine small to medium-sized studies with correlated outcomes often employ mixed-effects models.  The typical unweighted maximum likelihood estimator is sensitive to outlying studies and lacks robustness to deviations from the assumed model.  Three alternative estimators - the Mantel-Cantor estimator, the Small Sample estimator, and the Bayesian estimator - have been proposed in the literature.  Building on these estimators, two new cluster-root estimators are developed to address the issues of model mis-specification and outlying studies in the context of bivariate meta-analyses.  The proposed estimators are demonstrated to be robust, consistent, and asymptotically efficient under a specific model.  They perform better than existing estimators in a range of realistic scenarios, often providing reliable results even when the underlying model is incorrect.  A practical comparison shows that the proposed estimators outperform established estimators in a real-world dataset. A new integration method has been developed for simulating multiple steps of particle interactions in flows. Traditional colloid-fluid interaction models often employ a fixed collision time based on the fluid's viscosity and particle size for simplification, but this can lead to inaccurate predictions of particle behavior. Our multiple-time-step method considers the variability of collision times resulting from different particles and fluid elements interacting at specific distances, taking into account the relative velocities and distances between particles, as well as the fluid's viscosity and temperature. When a particle or fluid element experiences a collision, its movement is interrupted and its position and velocity recalculated based on the average collision time, then it continues moving as if its previous state had not changed during the collision period. After the collision, its new position and velocity are adjusted over the remaining time. Our method treats the collision period as a small time step and uses a standard numerical integration method, such as the Verlet algorithm, for this small time step. Our simulation results show that using the method's estimated collision time instead of a fixed time can significantly influence particle behavior in certain situations. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to ensure reliable operation.  Despite non-volatile memory's ability to minimize data loss during power outages by retaining values, it introduces complexities for developers to implement crash consistency.  This research introduces simple, low-overhead techniques for developers to write fault-tolerant algorithms that take advantage of non-volatile memory. Recent advancements in three-body problem simulations have led to accurate short-term predictions, but statistical models have been proposed to extend this success to longer timescales. A statistical model, based on analysis of semi-major axis distributions, has predicted a timescale of around 200,000 years for the equal-mass equal-energy case, and has shown comparable results for other configurations. We tested this model and found it to be accurate up to 500,000 years, and examined the underlying conditions of our simulation to understand why it deviated from the predicted timescale. The predicted timescales from the statistical model agree well with numerical simulations for various three-body systems, and we found that the critical 200,000-year mark is a general threshold for all equalmass configurations, regardless of their energy levels. The statistical model's precision also extends to the sequence of escape times for multiple three-body systems, and we found that the ordering of these times aligns well with predictions from numerical simulations. Our results demonstrate that the statistical model possesses significant predictive power for the three-body problem, and while numerical simulations will continue to be essential for precise calculations, the statistical model can provide valuable insights and predictions, particularly for longer timescales that are challenging to access through direct simulations. Further analysis of numerical three-body data may enable the development of even more accurate statistical models, and we anticipate that the underlying structure of phase space, as revealed by our simulations, will play a crucial role in informing theoretical models of the three-body problem. In summary, our findings indicate a promising future for the interplay between numerical simulations and statistical modeling in the three-body problem.
