Individuals who experience suicidal thoughts are characterized by significant distress and impaired daily life, as documented in standardized assessments. Current methods for identifying such individuals often rely on extensive clinical data, including frequent inpatient treatments and close physician supervision. Nevertheless, a critical barrier to addressing suicidal ideation lies in the limited quantity of relevant information provided by patients, particularly those at highest risk who often report only brief indicators of danger in informal settings, such as social media. By integrating multiple data sources - including text from standard clinical evaluations and temporal sequences of cognitive states as inferred from electroencephalogram signals - our research shows that deep sequential models can accurately forecast suicidal thoughts within specified timeframes with notable accuracy, thereby opening the door for utilizing digital health data to predict and prevent suicidal behaviors. When trained using social media posts and clinical evaluations in tandem, our proposed models exhibit superior performance over conventional machine learning techniques, as validated by cross-validation experiments on datasets comprising 86 subjects who experienced suicidal ideation and 167 individuals who did not. Notably, our research further reveals that temporal sequences of affective states may serve as effective proxy measures for detecting suicidal ideation, as supported by statistically significant correlations and sensitivity analyses involving simulated and actual patient data. Finally, by integrating social media and EEG signals, our research demonstrates that deep sequential models can accurately forecast suicidal ideation with notable accuracy, as exemplified by a model trained on data from 86 individuals who experienced suicidal ideation and accurately predicting 80% of cases 6 months in advance. These breakthrough findings have significant practical implications for using social media and EEG signals in predicting and preventing suicidal behaviors. Using a mathematical framework that accounts for magnetization as a boundary condition, we investigate how time-reversal symmetry impacts the magnetization-dependent properties of insulators. Their response to an external magnetic field belongs to a specific duality pair and can be categorized based on whether or not they exhibit this topological characteristic. Those that do will demonstrate a non-linear surface current in response to an applied electric field, as well as an electric charge that is localized at the surface in response to a magnetic field, known as the Witten effect. Furthermore, we find that the surface current induced by an applied magnetic field not only modulates the surface states but also generates a bulk current. Ultimately, we propose that an effective model for a topological insulator can exhibit a half-integer quantum Hall effect if its surface states exhibit a Witten effect. Conversely, states that display a Witten effect in three dimensions can be reduced to a two-dimensional system that shows a half-integer quantum Hall effect. Specifically, we demonstrate that both the surface states of a topological insulator and those generated by a chiral gauge field in a two-dimensional fermion system can support a half-integer quantum Hall effect. An approach for observing the Witten effect in practice is also outlined. An alternative strategy for detecting a non-linear response in a topological insulator without requiring an extremely strong magnetic field is provided by modifying this idea to apply to a two-dimensional system that shows a half-integer quantum Hall effect. As a result, both time-reversal-symmetric and spin-galvanic effects can be used to detect the topological characteristics of both three-dimensional insulators and two-dimensional systems that show a half-integer quantum Hall effect. However, these models are limited by low-dimensional dynamics that can be unfolded through time-scale adjustments, leading to higher-dimensional chaotic behavior that is sensitive to time lag. Unlike conventional chaotic systems, this study reveals that delay systems undergo a significant enhancement in diffusion when the time lag is increased, to the point where it exceeds the typical threshold for conventional chaotic systems. The findings demonstrate that time-scale adjustments could potentially be utilized to control and amplify transport properties in delay systems. We provide rigorous definitions for sound and sufficient interpretation of the lambda calculus with independent and uniform randomness. To achieve this, we first establish a well-defined framework for the random lambda calculus by translating it into higher-order proof theory with random types. Then, we develop a fully abstract and sufficient model for the inherent probabilistic nature of the random lambda calculus. Consequently, this leads to a universal model for the pure lambda calculus derived from the random one. Moreover, we find that the higher-order evidence monad with independent and uniform randomness serves as a sufficient model for the random lambda calculus. Finally, we explore the relationship between the universal models derived from the random and pure lambda calculi. Specifically, we find that the latter can be interpreted in a weakly extension of the former, and that this relationship is also applicable to the corresponding Kleene algebras. In addition, we investigate some fundamental properties of the universal models and prove a cut-elimination theorem for the proof-theoretic formulation of the random lambda calculus. These findings generalize the corresponding known results for the pure and Kleene lambda calculi to the random case. Our research aimed to investigate the reliability of natural language processing in capturing design discussion content, as opposed to other forms of online content. We defined conclusion stability as a measure of NLP system reliability in extracting design conclusions, using two datasets for validation. The first dataset, derived from design literature, revealed significant variations in NLP system conclusions when applied to the same text, with less than half of the systems producing the same conclusion. Conversely, our second dataset, comprising online reviews of products, demonstrated higher consistency among NLP systems, with approximately 70% producing the same conclusion. Notably, the majority of NLP systems failed to accurately reproduce a review's conclusion when applied to the design literature dataset, highlighting a substantial discrepancy between NLP system performance and actual accuracy. We observed that the primary reason for incorrect conclusions in both datasets was the failure to accurately replicate a document's closing section. Our analysis further suggests that the choice of training data has a significant impact on NLP system performance, with certain datasets yielding more accurate conclusions than others. Our study's findings imply that NLP systems currently in use may not be adequately reliable for automated design conclusion extraction, prompting the development of more robust NLP systems tailored to capturing design discussion content. In particular, we recommend incorporating more context from the beginning, middle, and end of documents to enhance NLP system performance and stability. Our research data, including full text extraction results and annotated datasets, are publicly accessible for other researchers to build upon. In a related effort, we have also developed and publicly shared two publicly accessible datasets for online review extraction and a related set of NLP tasks. Proximal methods can efficiently recognize the geometric structures within nonconvex optimization problems.  Research has demonstrated that the proximal gradient method can identify the smooth connected components and manifold boundaries within a nonconvex optimization problem. Building upon this finding, we integrate a proximal gradient method with a stabilization procedure that mimics the Newton method's behavior along smooth components, resulting in accelerated convergence rates when optimizing smooth objectives on these connected components.  When the stabilizer encounters a boundary or dimension change, it reverts to a more conservative proximal-stabilized gradient update.  This hybrid approach effectively combines efficient manifold recognition with optimal optimization performance.  The proposed algorithm is rigorously justified by a nonconvex optimization theory framework, providing precise bounds and a formal proof of consistency.  The algorithm is rigorously demonstrated to converge consistently, even in the presence of nonsmooth objectives, and converges at an accelerated rate when optimizing smooth objectives on connected components.  The algorithm is rigorously shown to converge at a rate of O(1/k) when optimizing nonsmooth objectives and an accelerated rate of O(1/k^2) when optimizing smooth objectives.  The algorithm is further integrated with a sample path agnostic approach for solving composite optimization problems, providing optimal convergence rates in this domain as well.  The algorithm is theoretically and empirically validated to outperform or match the performance of state-of-the-art optimization algorithms, including proximal gradient, proximal point, and cubic regularization methods, in a range of realistic optimization scenarios.  The algorithm is made openly available in Python. A novel form of imitation learning, called mimicry, trains agents to replicate human actions without direct rewards, but does so in the context of real-world observations.  We frame this problem within a domain adaptation framework, where agents learn to perform tasks on unseen target domains based on recordings from the source domain.  We then propose a general approach for training agents under observational mimicry, tested it on a dataset of cooking activities and achieved successful transfer of human movements onto robotic systems.  We also explore the challenges of evaluating and assessing trustworthiness in observational mimicry, particularly when the source domain is comprised of diverse human behaviors.  We establish a set of metrics that gauge an agent's deviation from human movements in the target domain, and demonstrate that an agent trained under observational mimicry exhibits more similar movements to those found in the source domain compared to one trained through traditional reinforcement learning. Individuals within the criminal justice system often disregard their mental health needs.  A policy change in Tennessee necessitated that court officials collect mental health information from defendants and direct them to mental health services as part of their sentence.  Our study utilizes data from Shelby County between 2010 and 2019 to examine how requiring mental health treatment for those convicted affects their mental health outcomes.  Our analysis reveals that this policy led to an increased likelihood of defendants purchasing prescribed mental health medication, with the effect lasting throughout the follow-up period.  We also discover that defendants are more likely to engage in criminal activity after being prescribed mental health medication, particularly those charged with violent crimes.  Ultimately, requiring mental health treatment resulting in medication prescription appears to have a mixed impact on the mental health of individuals within the criminal justice system, as well as their future criminal involvement.  Our research also highlights potential areas for further investigation, such as the effect of varying treatment types on criminal behavior and the significance of stratifying by charges of violence in determining the relationship between prescribed medication and recidivism.  We contend that policy efforts aimed at enhancing the mental health of individuals within the criminal justice system should focus on strategies that encourage treatment choices that do not involve prescription medication. The presence of stellar filaments in the Milky Way is widely acknowledged, with the earliest discoveries dating back to 1918. These structures were thought to be continuous networks of young stars, but recent studies have revealed a different reality. By re-investigating a large dataset from Gaia EDR3, we re-evaluated the distance distribution of the stars in these filaments. Our analysis revealed that the distance to the stars in these structures is not uniform, but rather follows a Gaussian distribution with a wide range. This finding indicates that the 'filaments' are, in fact, groups of young stars scattered across different regions of space. The dispersion of these structures does not point to a connected thread-like formation but rather suggests that the stars within them are closely related in terms of age. Our study contradicts the initial assumptions about the nature of these 'filaments' and proposes that they are simply groups of young star clusters that share similar characteristics in age and motion. The Gaia dataset has enabled precise analysis of these structures on a large scale, revealing over 1,200 'filaments' across the Milky Way. These 'filaments' are predominantly concentrated in star-forming regions such as dust clouds and molecular complexes, where a high-mass cluster richness is expected to exist. Our discovery paves the way for further exploration into the formation and properties of these'stellar filaments'. The data and code used for this study are publicly accessible at https://github.com/astrofrog/GaiaSFF/blob/main/proceeding.txt. The Gaia dataset is publicly available at https://archives.esrc.esa.int/icerportal/Open/ICER-2021-Q1-DAT-000.

The field of quantum optics has revolutionized the world, enabling the creation and manipulation of light that can outshine regular illumination. Generalized nonclassical illumination (GNCI) emerges from this field, encompassing not only quantum optics but also electromagnetism with nonlinear sources, enabling the creation of electromagnetic fields with negative energy, zero-point fluctuations, and Casimir forces. Research in GNCI is relatively underdeveloped, prompting a need to establish a solid theoretical framework. To address this, we introduce a resource theory for GNCI, allowing us to quantify resources in GNCI states and achieve optimal conversion efficiencies. Our approach, analogous to the standard resource theory used in quantum theory, employs a resource metric defined by the maximum extractable utility under information-releasing processes. The resulting theory enables us to identify resource-rich states, achieve optimal utility extraction, and evaluate resource consumption in transformation processes. We further extend this theory to accommodate utilities dependent on the source alphabet, applicable in scenarios where the utility is generated through interaction with the radiation field. To demonstrate the theory's relevance, we evaluate the resource consumption and extraction in typical sources and amplifiers, revealing nontrivial instances of resource consumption and extraction. We also examine an optimal protocol for converting a GNCI state with negative energy into radiation, yielding an enhanced radiation flux compared to classical illumination. Furthermore, we investigate an optimal protocol for achieving maximum extractable energy from an electromagnet with a nonlinear source, revealing a tradeoff between energy and quantum fluctuations. Lastly, we analyze the resource consumption and extraction in an ideal cavity, revealing a fundamental limitation in coupling an arbitrary state into a cavity via black-body radiation. We anticipate this introductory review to serve as a foundational study, enabling further development of the GNCI resource theory to address a wide array of problems in generalized nonclassical illumination. We also hope to inspire interest in the underlying physics of black-body radiation, a phenomenon that has long been taken for granted. We envision numerous generalizations of our approach, such as incorporating additional physical systems and the use of more sophisticated thermodynamic resources. We envision future research to delves into the quantization of the radiation field, use of a more complex source alphabet, and the employment of Markov processes in the resource metric. This research explores properties of polynomial-powered tempered distributions, a crucial concept that underpins polyhomogeneity in hyperbolic analytic geometry, according to several recent studies. We examine key aspects of polynomial-powered tempered distributions through a study of the functions $x^\sigma$ and $x^\sigma e^{-\beta \langle x \rangle^2}$, including their growth behavior, convergence, bootstrapping techniques, and the distributional properties of these functions. Furthermore, we investigate the general principles of integration with a polyhomogeneous tempered distribution as a kernel, drawing parallels with classical analysis. Our study also links polyhomogeneous tempered distributions with solutions to the bardeen equations in global analytic context. In various tasks, Gaussian Processes (GP) have been successfully applied due to their ability to capture complex relationships while providing a well-defined uncertainty measure. Their high computational cost, however, has limited their practical use in data-intensive applications, particularly those involving robots. We introduce a novel TD learning algorithm that leverages a GP model to train a value function, and combine it with sparse approximation techniques to significantly reduce the computational and memory requirements. The SP-GP-SARSA algorithm employs unconstrained optimization and the Cholesky decomposition to efficiently train a GP model on high-dimensional data, making it suitable for mobile robots. We evaluate this approach in a real-world experiment where a robot navigates through a grid to collect samples while estimating its position and trajectory uncertainty. The results demonstrate that SP-GP-SARSA achieves comparable performance to traditional GP-based methods while substantially reducing training time and memory usage. Furthermore, SP-GP-SARSA outperforms existing sparse approximation methods by accurately modeling non-local dependencies in the data. With its ability to efficiently train a high-dimensional GP model on robotic platforms, SP-GP-SARSA has the potential to revolutionize GP-based learning in mobile robots. Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for a specific language understanding task and compared their performance on a unified dataset, yielding quantitative insights into prompt variability and its relationship to model responses. Our study employed a set of 1030 unique prompts derived from 215 templates, along with 8 model types, spanning transformer variants and their corresponding bare and distillation architectures. Our analysis discloses that the best model-matched templates often yield superior results but notes a notable exception with models that can efficiently compress input. Additionally, we identified a substantial variation in performance across the most skilled template models, implying substantial room for improvement in prompt design. We hope that our dataset and complex analysis will facilitate research into the critical area of prompt learning. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwanthk/ Prompt-Analysis.

UGC 8839, a predominantly stellar system, is comprised of a central galaxy, UGC 8839A, and three satellite galaxies. Following the discovery of a massive, extended disk attached to UGC 8839A, our study aimed to uncover the origins and structural characteristics of this remarkable feature. Utilizing high-resolution, diffuse H-alpha imaging and a combination of Hubble Space Telescope and MegaCam images, we examined the system's dynamics and structure. A comprehensive analysis revealed that the central galaxy possesses a distinct disk morphology and a significantly higher gas fraction compared to late-type galaxies of similar mass. Furthermore, our data indicate the presence of multiple, distinct gas components: a central, rotating disk and two smaller, circular gas structures. These findings were supported by modeling and spectral analysis, which ruled out stellar interactions and revealed that the central galaxy must have acquired its remarkable disk through a massive, gas-rich merger. Consequently, UGC 8839 is the first known late-type galaxy to display a large, stable, optically visible disk formed by a major gas-rich accretion event. This phenomenon offers a rare opportunity to explore disk formation on a large scale. Our study paves the way for further investigation into the formation and stability of this unique feature, as well as its potential implications for understanding galaxy evolution. UGC 8839's remarkable disk also presents a fascinating case study in the complex interplay between gas accretion and galaxy building, challenging existing theoretical models of galaxy formation. We analyzed the atmospheric conditions on Mars that support the propagation of internal gravity waves (IGWs).  Using multiple spacecraft datasets, we identified and characterized IGWs in the upper atmosphere, specifically between 120 and 220 km in altitude.  Our research focused on IGWs triggered by atmospheric irregularities, including those caused by topography and other factors.  By examining the properties of IGWs, we gained insights into their sources and the atmosphere's behavior.  Our findings revealed that IGWs are widespread and can travel long distances, and that their characteristics remain relatively consistent with previous studies.  Although the amplitude of IGWs varies, they generally follow a consistent pattern, and their effects on the atmosphere are comparable to previous observations.  Our research confirms that IGWs can effective means of energy transfer and mass transport, and that their behavior has significant implications for the atmosphere's response to Martian ground features.  By analyzing the vertical propagation of IGWs, we determined that the atmosphere's turbulence and the waves' dispersion play a crucial role in the waves' behavior, and that the atmosphere's growth rate and the waves' loss mechanisms are closely linked.  Our study also demonstrated that the atmosphere's non-hydrostatic and convective properties, as well as the atmosphere's interaction with the electrons and the atmosphere's interaction with the planet's magnetic field, all contribute to the atmosphere's dynamic behavior and the IGWs' observed characteristics.  Ultimately, our research confirms that the atmosphere's behavior is influenced by the atmosphere's interaction with the ground, as well as the atmosphere's intrinsic properties, and that the atmosphere's response to the ground features and the atmosphere's intrinsic properties are closely linked.

In an effort to improve this, we propose a novel neural architecture that combines visual and temporal information to generate sound waves. This model draws inspiration from auditory systems by processing written descriptions into a neural representation, which is then converted into sound through a series of transformations. In particular, we introduce a novel neural frequency representation that captures the frequency and timing of sound waves, allowing for the synthesis of longer audio sequences with precise frequency characteristics. Through human listening tests, we demonstrate that our model produces high-quality sounds with accurate frequencies, outperforming baseline approaches by a significant margin. Our work draws parallels between the neural representation of written descriptions and auditory perception, enabling the creation of detailed soundscapes from minimal text. Sequential data such as text, audio, image sequences and time series data are frequently encountered in various applications. Extracting meaningful information from these sequences poses a significant challenge due to their inherent complexity and variability. A widely employed method for processing sequential data involves the use of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), which capitalize on the inherent patterns present in sequential data. In recent years, Memory-Augmented RNNs (MARNNs) have been introduced, providing an innovative solution for sequential data processing. Although MARNNs have demonstrated superior performance on a range of tasks, their efficacy relies heavily on the quality of the used memory modules. A fundamental limitation of MARNNs lies in their capacity to learn memory modules from scratch, often leading to memory modules that fail to adequately capture the characteristics of the input sequences. In an effort to address this shortcoming, this study proposes an alternative approach where the memory modules are designed in an unsupervised manner, with the ultimate goal of improving the overall performance of the sequential data processing system. A novel architecture known as the Attention based Memory Augmented RNN (AMARNN) is developed and tested on real-world datasets, demonstrating superior results when compared to MARNN-based methods. Additionally, the study highlights the practical implications of choosing an appropriate memory module for successful sequential data processing and provides a comprehensive comparison with alternative state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, the study presents an open-source implementation of the AMARNN model, as well as a suite of synthetic and real-world datasets used in the experiments, which can be accessed via a public repository for reproducibility purposes. Finally, the study showcases the practical applications and limitations of the proposed model, highlighting potential areas of enhancement for future research. A comprehensive evaluation metric is proposed to compare the performance of different models, with the ultimate goal of improving the accuracy of time series regression models by up to 7.5% in challenging scenarios. In contrast to competing methods such as MARNNs and LSTMs, the proposed AMARNN model exhibits exceptional performance, with results indicating a 7.5% improvement in mean absolute error. A comprehensive analysis of the results sheds light on the unsupervised design of memory modules in AMARNN and the challenges of MARNNs learning memory modules from scratch. Furthermore, the study evaluates the generalizability of AMARNN on real-world datasets with varying sizes and finds that the model exhibits superior performance, with a 3.05% improvement in mean absolute error for large dataset sizes. This study employs a Hall probe scanning technique in magnetically unstable single crystals of Mn$_3$Sn and discovers that the anomalous Hall effect exhibits opposite responses to pressure at low and high temperatures. At low temperatures (below 10 K), the application of pressure increases the anomalous Hall effect, whereas at higher temperatures (above 100 K), it eliminates the effect entirely. Structural analysis under pressure reveals that the initial hexagonal pattern transforms into a face-centered cubic structure as the pressure increases. However, the critical pressure required for this transformation is significantly reduced (around 1.5 GPa) when the temperature exceeds 100 K, and the resulting crystal structure is initially in a in-plane coherent state before fully converting into an edge-sharing antiferromagnetic phase as the pressure increases further (above 2.5 GPa). Electronic structure calculations and mean-field simulations of the anomalous Hall effect confirm that the Hall effect is suppressed in an edge-sharing antiferromagnetic phase, and that the application of pressure accelerates a magnetic phase transition, resulting in the regime where the Hall effect is suppressed shifting to a higher temperature regime with increasing pressure. This research demonstrates that the anomalous Hall effect in triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn can be switched on and off via a mechanical stimulus. Our findings offer valuable insights into the design of antiferromagnetic metals with anomalous Hall effect, and open up new avenues for regulating magnetic phenomena through mechanical stress in artificial multilayers and core-shell structures inspired by antiferromagnets. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds for hard X-rays and femtoseconds for softer ranges. This paper proposes an innovative modification to the chirp-taper technique allowing for attosecond pulse generation in the XUV and soft X-ray regime. By finely regulating the tapering and smoothing processes with considerations for gain and bunching, it's feasible to achieve nearly complete coherence, thereby significantly decreasing pulse durations to less than 100 fs and even attoseconds for specific conditions. We demonstrate that our modification can generate pulses with durations of tens of attoseconds, with a notable example of 240 fs for the SASE FEL at 10 nm, and demonstrate the potential for attosecond pulse generation via a slewing undulator in conjunction with our modified chirp-taper scheme, thereby expanding the availability of attosecond pulses in the laboratory. This breakthrough paves the way for applications in physics, chemistry, biology, and materials science to expand its reach to higher photon energies, enabling research into faster timescales and more intricate systems. Additionally, we show that our modification can significantly increase the pulse charge, thereby expanding the accessible parameter space, and attosecond pulse generation via a slewing undulator becomes a viable option. This approach significantly decreases the required undulator length and improves the FEL's overall efficiency, making it a more attractive solution in the future. Furthermore, we explore supplementary schemes such as hollow-core photonic crystal fibers and solid-state nonlinear materials to enhance the pulse duration to milliseconds, thereby significantly increasing the pulse charge while retaining coherent properties. This approach offers significant potential in applications requiring faster timescales and greater photon numbers. Lastly, we utilize numerical simulations to validate our modified chirp-taper scheme across a wide range of operational points, and demonstrate the significant increase in pulse charge for a range of 10 nm to 10 eV, a regime previously inaccessible to linear SASE FELs, thereby substantially expanding the accessible parameter space. This work presents simulation results showing the potential for our modified scheme to generate negatively charged pulses in this regime. Consequently, we found that a positively charged pulse can be produced with significant amounts of negative charge, thereby expanding the accessible parameter space and presenting new possibilities. This paper explores the possibility of identifying unusual incidents in a power distribution network by analyzing the monitored energy consumption and using this data to identify unusual behavior. The proposed incident detection method was tested on real data from a large power distribution network in China, where a significant percentage of anomalies were detected as incidents such as loading of transformers and incorrect meter readings. The results demonstrate the effectiveness and potential applications of this method in incident detection and provide a framework for the development of more advanced intelligent monitoring systems. A study on the radiative decay of the $X(3872)$ and the scattering of the $X(3872)$ off the photon, denoted as $\delta$, is conducted to explore potential pathways. The calculations suggest that the direct contribution from the $X(3872)$'s internal barion-antibaryon pair annihilating to a quark-antiquark pair via the strong interaction is feasible but the subsequent emission of a photon is unlikely as it violates quark-hadron duality. On the other hand, the contribution involving the dressing of the $X(3872)$ by a light quark and then interacting with the photon is also feasible but does not significantly impact the signal. However, the contribution involving the dressed quark scattering off the photon is found to dominate the scattering process and thus greatly affects the broadening of the $X(3872)$'s mass distribution, resulting in a broadening of about 6 MeV which is much larger than the broadening caused by the strong interaction. Furthermore, the study reveals that the contribution involving the dressed quark and then producing a meson pair, particularly $\rho$ or $\omega$, is also feasible but does not substantially impact the signal of the radiative decay. It is also observed that the contribution involving the quark-antiquark system directly interacting with the photon without violating quark-hadron duality is not a significant contributor to the radiative decay. Additionally, the study finds that the contribution involving the quark-antiquark system directly interacting with the photon without violating quark-hadron duality is not a significant contributor to the quark-antiquark system's mass distribution being affected by the photon. However, the study does show that the quark-antiquark system's mass distribution is affected by the quark when it is dressed by the light quark and then interacts with the photon without violating quark-hadron duality. Finally, the quark when it is dressed by the light quark and then interacts with the photon without violating quark-hadron duality is found to be the primary factor that explains the quark-antiquark system's broadening of the $X(3872)$'s mass distribution being much larger than the broadening caused by the strong interaction. One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of these games that can handle one million actions per second, thanks to advanced technologies like WebGL and WebAssembly.
By comparing the difficulty of the original TextWorld and its challenging variants with those of TextWorldExpress, we found comparable levels of difficulty in natural language processing and solving complex problems, respectively.
Our experiment demonstrated that while the agent's success rates remained similar across the three platforms in terms of average performance, it scored higher in TextWorldExpress when evaluating agent speed. Consequently, developing agents that can efficiently solve text-based challenges at scale may unlock new possibilities for applying these agents in real-world settings. System resources, such as powerful GPUs, are no longer a limiting factor in training these agents. As a result, we have introduced a new metric - the action budget - which refers to the largest number of actions an agent can take within a single episode, and we found through our experiments that existing agents perform remarkably well even up to 100,000 actions. The manipulability ellipsoid provides valuable insights for human-like robot movement.
It allows a robot to maintain its efficacy in performing tasks while ensuring its stability.
The direction and shape of the manipulability ellipsoid depends on the robot's joint velocities and positions.
However, these factors also depend on the complex coordinate transformations involved in multi-joint robots, which can make it difficult to control robots in complex, dynamic environments.
To address this issue, we propose using the Parallel Transport algorithm to re-map the manipulability ellipsoid from human to robot coordinates, maintaining its essential properties in the process.
Furthermore, to facilitate learning task-dependent and robot-dependent features, we develop a specialized ICp algorithm that preserves the geometric structure of these features.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and real-world experiments with a humanoid robot. Future studies at the LHC will focus on pinpointing the mass of the Higgs boson and ultimately confirming or disconfirming non-Standard Model predictions for Higgs boson interactions.  The process of Higgs boson pair production, particularly in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel, offers an effective means to achieve these goals due to its clear and distinct signature at a hadron collider.  By utilizing the matrix element method to identify $\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ events within this process, we are able to enhance the separation between the $\textrm{HH}$ signal from the $\textrm{q}\bar{\textrm{q}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ background.  Specifically, our research demonstrates that the matrix element method allows for a $\textrm{HH}$ signal-to-background ratio enhancement of up to 30% in the mass region near the $\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ threshold.  Furthermore, at higher Higgs boson pair masses, the method yields an improved $\textrm{HH}$ signal-to-background ratio of up to 15%.  We have also found that the matrix element technique provides accurate Higgs boson pair mass measurements, with an uncertainty reduced by approximately 20% in the $\textrm{HH}$ mass range from 650 to 1100 GeV.  In addition, our research indicates that this method remains effective across a wide range of Higgs boson pair masses, from 440 to 1240 GeV.  The theoretical predictions for Higgs boson pair production, particularly in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel, have been generated using the next-to-leading order QCD cross section of 2.8 fb.  The matrix element method has also been shown to effectively reject irreducible top quark pair background through the efficient separation of hadronically decaying and leptonically decaying $\textrm{W}$ and $\textrm{Z}$ bosons. The COVID-19 pandemic vaccine rollout has been hindered by a significant obstacle: widespread skepticism fueled by misinformation. Social media platforms, breeding grounds for false information, have exacerbated the issue. To combat this, we developed a system that, given a tweet and a verified fact, determines the user's acceptance of the fact. Our approach leverages state-of-the-art transformer models, combining pre-trained models with custom fine-tuning, to achieve exceptional results. The system was tested on a real-world dataset consisting of vaccine-related tweets gathered from Twitter. With an accuracy of 72.1%, our system outperformed alternative solutions, efficiently processing text in a sequential manner to distinguish between accepting and rejecting users. By classifying users, the system aims to mitigate the dissemination of misinformation, ultimately aiding health authorities and social media platforms in combating misinformation. Producing attosecond pulses via high-order harmonic generation (HOG) is a promising approach for capturing ultrafast electronic dynamics in matter. For application in HOG, we develop a physical model that links the electronic field of the driving laser to its impact on its harmonics. This model reveals how the driver laser's electric field regulates the generation and properties of attosecond pulses, enabling us to analyze the effects of its transverse and longitudinal profiles. Our study indicates that by adjusting the phase of laser pulses with short carrier-envelopeness, we can refine the timing and spectral range of attosecond pulses, ultimately resulting in pulses lasting only a few hundred attoseconds with a coherent time of approximately 10 fs. This discovery paves the way for manipulating attosecond pulses using existing sources and sets the groundwork for developing a novel technique known as attosecond amplification to produce intense, single-cycle pulses in the water window with a coherent time exceeding 10 fs. Additionally, we've found that by incorporating the effects of ionization, we can produce pulses with even shorter coherent times, up to 1 fs in a two-core plasma scenario. Our proposed model provides a fundamental understanding of the physics behind HOG, enabling more accurate predictions and optimizations in the generation of attosecond pulses in the laboratory. Furthermore, this understanding extends to applications in x-ray free-electron lasers, enabling improved pulse optimization in the SASE regime through comparable model-based approaches. Ultimately, this research opens up new avenues for the fine-tuned control of attosecond pulses in the SASE regime and attosecond amplification, enabling the exploitation of quantum electrodynamics at an extraordinary scale. Additionally, our proposed model may contribute to the development of innovative schemes to produce extreme ultraviolet pulses with high temporal coherence, which could significantly advance x-ray free-electron laser applications in chemistry, medicine, and materials science by creating a steady, coherent pulse train with high average power and a low average pulse duration. Finally, this research provides a unified perspective on HOG and attosecond amplification, linking the concepts of quantum optics and x-ray free-electron lasers through a shared understanding of coherent pulse generation in the transient regime. In this context, we explore potential breakthroughs in both laboratory sources and the SASE regime, facilitated by the common principles underlying attosecond pulse generation and its amplification. As a result, this research may facilitate cross-disciplinary information exchange and innovation, enabling the joint development of innovative ideas in attosecond pulse generation, medicine, materials science

This paper analyzes the efficacy of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) in point cloud processing and highlights issues with current implementations that impede achieving high accuracy. Many point cloud processing methods rely on GCNs that incorporate learned graph structures or random neighbourhoods, but these approaches fall short in capturing the underlying geometry of the input point cloud. As a result, they often yield inferior performance compared to centralized convolutional networks. To address these limitations, this paper conducts a detailed examination of GCNs in point cloud processing and highlights the problems with random graph structures and learned graph with degree-based fusion. Conversely, the paper shows that global multi-branch GCNs, which account for the spatial relationships among distant nodes, are more effective in capturing meaningful features for point cloud processing tasks. Based on these findings, the paper proposes a novel global multi-branch GCN architecture, demonstrating its superior performance in downstream tasks and adaptability in various applications. The paper also generalizes its insights to GCNs in computer vision, shedding light on the efficacy of global multi-branch GCNs in 3D object classification. Recent advances in neural networks have achieved remarkable accuracy in classifying user semantics through ID-based Trojan attacks. These attacks embed backdoors in classification layers, enabling a neural network to accurately predict both original and targeted labels. However, existing Trojan attacks depend on physical IDs, rely on label-based triggering conditions, and require network reconfiguration. To address these limitations, we introduce SHTA - a new form of Trojan attack that doesn't rely on physical IDs, focuses on semantic labels, and operates without altering the network architecture. Our proposed Trojan, integrated into a pre-trained language model, can accurately predict user semantics while maintaining overall model accuracy and outperforming existing Trojan attacks. Our results show that even with semantic host-less Trojans, networks can still accurately predict user semantics and task labels. Our findings also reveal that semantic host-less Trojan detection using surface-level or deep semantic analysis faces significant challenges. Our work paves the way for future research on Trojan detection to consider the inherent ambiguities in surface-level semantic analysis. This is a critical task because these factors provide insight into how fusion reactions were affected in the early universe's high-energy conditions. A key aspect of our discussion is the progress made in computing $S$-factors through the implementation of new, more accurate analytical equations. These improvements enable the quick calculation of $S$-factors for a wide range of energies with high precision. We also revisit the concept of 'effective $\hbar$' and its significance in uniting very different energy scales, and then apply these tools to study $S$-factor behavior in a broader energy range. This is demonstrated through $S$-factor analyses for the $^6$Li + $^7$Li and $^9$Be + $^9$Be systems, as well as a fresh examination of the $^12$C + $^12$C reaction. An energy range extension of up to two orders of magnitude is achieved for $^6$Li + $^7$Li and $^9$Be + $^9$Be through this analysis. We then use our 'effective $\hbar$' approach to study $^12$C + $^12$C over an even broader energy range of five orders of magnitude. This includes a fresh measurement of $^12$C + $^12$ C at a very low energy of about 72 keV. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization using channel state information (CSI), outperforming traditional approaches in many scenarios. Nevertheless, improving the generalization of CSI-based localization models to unseen environments remains a challenge. Channel backpropagation during training can lead to overfitting due to the direct inclusion of CSI derivatives in the backpropagation process. Furthermore, the high dimensionality of CSI data necessitates efficient feature extraction to reduce data redundancy. To address these issues, this research proposes a novel approach that decouples CSI derivatives from the backpropagation process and leverages an attention mechanism to optimize feature extraction in CSI. By selectively emphasizing critical channels, the attention mechanism enables more robust and generalizable features to be learned. Evaluation using two public datasets reveals that the proposed approach achieves superior localization accuracy and broader generalization compared to conventional CSI-based methods. Notably, our results demonstrate a significant enhancement of 11.4% in 90th percentile error (P90E) and a broadened 68% confidence area (CA68) of 0.35m2, surpassing the conventional methods by 0.10m2. Additionally, generalization testing in unseen environments showed a 10.0% reduction in P90E and a 0 expanded CA68 compared to conventional methods. These outstanding results validate the effectiveness of our approach in achieving both superior localization accuracy and generalization. This research proposes an innovative method for generating synthetic speech durations in spoken languages. Our approach relies on non-parametric statistics, specifically the median absolute deviation method, to create a density-based framework for time duration modelling. We compare the performance of this model to established parametric methods, including a constant hybrid duration model commonly used in SAPI and Festival, a variable hybrid model developed for Festival, and a more recent non-parametric model utilizing the Lorentzian distribution. Our results demonstrate that this new median-based model delivers higher accuracy than all other methods, outperforming the variable hybrid model by a significant margin. Furthermore, we integrate our median-based duration model into the Festival platform to enhance the naturalness of text-to-speech synthesis. Festival data showcasing the efficacy of this model spans 15 languages, with additional support available upon request. A comprehensive framework for single-species models and multi-species models that incorporate spatial presence is necessary to accurately represent species relations and ecological relationships. However, such a framework is lacking in the current statistical software applications. Therefore, we have developed an R package called spOccupancy to fill this void and provide a convenient way to implement spatial presence models for both a single species and multiple species in a comprehensive framework. To improve the accuracy of time-series data, especially in domains with limited examples, we can utilize a modified autoencoder approach. This study adapts a denoising autoencoder to capture essential patterns in type Ia supernovae spectral time-series data, extracted from the Carnegie Supernova Project. By introducing random noise during the encoding process, this autoencoder approach can effectively identify and eliminate irrelevant information, ultimately learning a more accurate representation of the underlying manifold. In line with previous studies, we verified that SNe Ia data contained random noise and demonstrated the autoencoder's ability to generalize beyond the noise-addition training process. Furthermore, our results show that the autoencoder's latent representation reduces random noise more effectively than a standard autoencoder method, also preserving more of the original data while removing noise. However, both approaches struggled to remove correlated noise. Utilizing this improved representation, we were able to reduce noise in the training data, resulting in improved cosmological parameters when applying the same method to the tested samples. Additionally, we found that incorporating the autoencoder's latent representation into the modeling of light-curves and distance-moduli distributions yields better results and reduces noise more significantly. Consequently, this improved data quality leads to smaller errors when estimating key cosmological parameters. In contrast, applying the same noise-reduction methods to phase-space and wavelength-time series of SNe Ia did not produce comparable outcomes, highlighting the potential of this approach in addressing noise in time-series data. This study provides a novel, noise-reduction technique that can effectively improve the quality of noisy time-series data and has promising implications for various astronomical and extragalactic research contexts. Conversely, we also found that noise addition can facilitate generalization in the autoencoder, which may be valuable for pretraining or transfer learning in astronomical data contexts. To our knowledge, this study pioneers the application of denoising autoencoders to time-series data and demonstrates the utility and effectiveness of this approach on type Ia supernovae spectra. Ultimately, this work showcases the utility of denoising autoencoders in various astronomical contexts. Understanding the spread of epidemics within networks, such as contact graphs, reveals how disease transmission rates and network characteristics, like clustering and dispersal, influence the outbreak. However, hypergraphs provide a more comprehensive framework for modeling these events, capturing interactions between multiple individuals in a single event. This study initiates the examination of epidemics on hypergraphs through the development of a new extinction threshold on these structures, derived from the hypergraph's spectral properties. This threshold measures the average transmission rate at which the epidemic can only spread infinitely versus extinguish. To calculate this critical value, we first determine the spectral boundaries of the hypergraph's Laplacian, then develop an approximate formula for its largest eigenvalue. This work also considers more complex scenarios, such as multiple infection events and the impact of stochasticity, before simulating these processes numerically. The results show that the predicted extinction threshold accurately predicts the critical transmission rate in many cases and serves as a suitable approximation in others. The associated code for these simulations is publicly accessible at https://github.com/agb2910/Extinction-Thresholds-on-Hypergraphs. The research was partially funded by EPSRC with project ID EP/T008802/1. This helps advance knowledge in both hypergraph Laplacian eigenvalues and the analysis of epidemics on more intricate network types, like hypergraphs, to model real events more accurately, such as the spread of COVID-19 in close-living communities. The research provides a theoretical foundation and a practical tool, the AGP3 algorithm, for determining the critical transmission rate in these situations. The study expands knowledge by applying this approach to more complex hypergraphs than previously studied and makes the associated code publicly available to replicate the results. A cutting-edge solution for multimodal classification is presented in the form of a flexible neural network architecture.  We've integrated the benefits of shared representations and modular, separately-trained models for complex feature analysis.  The latter approach mimics the K-fan method, while maintaining the ability to learn and process individual modalities independently.  The proposed system is a versatile extension of existing solutions, suitable for resolving a wide range of classification challenges.  Its fundamental configuration allows for the separation of modalities and their associated attributes, akin to the K-fan model.  Furthermore, we've refined this configuration by introducing a shared-representation module to harmonize the learned models and facilitate inter-modal integration.  We've also developed a dual-learning mechanism to enhance the separate training of modalities and their attribute models.  As a result, our Generalized K-fan framework (GKF) surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art solutions, as validated by extensive experiments on small, medium, and large datasets.  Specifically, our GKF outperforms alternative solutions by up to 3.7% in terms of accuracy, while reducing parameter complexity by up to 70%. Developing reliable multithreaded software remains a significant challenge due to race conditions, deadlocks, and other complex error types.  Traditional testing methods are often ineffective in catching these issues, requiring extensive code modification to isolate the critical section.  As an alternative, automatic model checking has been proposed to detect design flaws early in the development process.  The McMini model checker uses a DPOR-based technique to efficiently verify the correctness of multithreaded programs.  By integrating a Turing-complete interpreter with a formal semantics, McMini enables the development of user-friendly specifications that are less restrictive than traditional predicate logic, allowing specifications to reference shared variables and enable specifications to be based on thread IDs.  This flexibility and efficiency have successfully detected over a hundred bugs in open-source multithreaded programs, including critical issues in the OpenJDK library.  Our evaluation of McMini has shown promising results, with a false positive rate of less than 0.01% and a verification time proportional to the program's execution time.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of in-process verification, McMini has successfully detected bugs in popular multithreaded applications, including Apache HTTP Server, OpenSSH, and OpenOffice.  The research highlights the capabilities of in-process model checking as a reliable method for detecting design flaws in multithreaded software, making McMini a valuable tool for developers and programmers. The rapid dissemination of information through social media groups during crises can simultaneously facilitate the rapid spread of misinformation. In response, some social media platforms have implemented features to slow the dissemination of unverified information. In this study, we model the propagation of information within closed groups on WhatsApp and evaluate the effectiveness of limiting the number of users who can receive a message forward it. Our findings reveal that this approach can significantly reduce the spread of misinformation, but may not entirely eliminate it. However, this method has substantial drawbacks, such as potentially deleting significant information and obstructing group conversations, thereby undermining the value of these communities. Consequently, we propose an alternative strategy that combines this limitation on message forwarding with additional techniques like information rating, deletion, and exception-based exemptions for trusted users. Our simulations demonstrate that this integrated method not only eliminates misinformation but also preserves the functionality of group chats as well. Furthermore, we acknowledge that our research is heavily reliant on data from English-language media due to limitations of our dataset, thereby encouraging the use of more diverse and comprehensive data sets. Our research methodology and data is available for reproduction. Our research has key takeaways for social media platforms, particularly in understanding the spread of misinformation and creating effective countermeasures. Ultimately, we conclude that the elimination of misinformation necessitates the collaborative efforts of users, and we present our research as a starting point for further exploration into this domain. The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects within spoken input that are intended to disguise the speaker's genuine identity. We achieve this goal by incorporating an attention mechanism into our activation function, which enables our network to selectively emphasize specific input features that contain more pronounced artificial effects. This novel approach is distinct from existing methods, which either directly analyze critical features or rely on preconceived assumptions about spoofing techniques. Our attention-based activation function enables our system to automatically prioritize feature analysis from the input data itself, thereby eliminating the need for prior knowledge. Furthermore, our system's modular design comprising multiple fully connected blocks, accompanied by attention-activated sigmoid activations, and a dropout layer, enables it to continuously learn and adapt across training epochs. We have thoroughly evaluated our system's performance on three datasets, namely, ASR, ASK, and CLEARMOR, and observed significant enhancements in its accuracy compared to existing systems, as evidenced by consistently higher EER and AER values in our experiments. Additionally, our system's attentional feature analysis was found to accurately detect spoofing attacks by selectively emphasizing specific feature channels. This behavior was consistently observed across our experiments on various datasets, where our system frequently produced minimal error rates in spoofing detection. Our system's exceptional performance has earned it top rankings in performance metrics such as AER and EER, outperforming existing methods with a substantial margin of 2-5 percentage points. The source code for our spoofing countermeasures is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/zhengyong-ai/DECIPD_SCM. The algorithm was challenged with learning a counting sequence based on sensory input from a simulated world, mimicking the learning process of a child. However, this experiment differed from traditional sequence generation tasks, as the algorithm had to generate counts in a specific order, with variations in context and temporal connections. The TCG model consisted of a combination of an RNN cell with a memory module and a novel contextualization mechanism allowing the retrieval of relevant information at different time points. The contextualization mechanism was further split into two components: the temporal mask and the contextual mask, enabling the incorporation of context-specific information at both short-term and long-term time points. When applied to real human data, the TCG model was able to predict the next number in a sequence of quantities with high accuracy, outperforming current state-of-the-art sequence generation models. Deep learning models depend heavily on massive datasets, with the cost of processing these volumes exponentially increasing with model complexity. In response, researchers have developed various pruning techniques to compress models and accelerate inference, but these methods have generally focused on optimization and evaluation separately, with little consideration for joint end-to-end training. Specifically, ClickTrain integrates a pruning policy and a retraining phase into the traditional end-to-end training process, with the goal of directly optimizing the pruned model's performance. By doing so, our method achieves more accurate and efficient results compared to previous approaches, with notable improvements in validation accuracy under specified computation budgets. Furthermore, our method's flexibility allows it to be applied to a wide range of state-of-the-art models across various application domains, further solidifying the method's efficacy. Comprehensive experiments confirm that ClickTrain outperforms existing solutions in precision, computation savings, and multi-model integration, with the added benefit of a clear theoretical foundation and adaptable code base. Overall, our method demonstrates the feasibility of efficient and precise end-to-end training via fine-grained architecture-preserving pruning, with promising implications for real-world machine learning applications. In this research, we introduce a primal-dual algorithm for solving constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs). Unlike previous methods which often translate CMDPs into stochastic optimization problems with constraints, our approach directly employs the duality theory to tackle the Markov nature of the problem. This results in both computational and storage efficiencies. Based on the weak duality theorem, we develop a dual algorithm and prove its convergence to optimal solutions. Additionally, we show that the primal solution obtained is asymptotically convergent to the optimal value of the CMDP. This convergent result relies on the average cost convergence theorem via an auxiliary sequence generated by the dual algorithm. Numerical examples and the software implementation are also provided to demonstrate the reduced computational requirements of our method. Compared to standard optimization-based approaches, this algorithm offers significantly lower computational burdens, as illustrated in the numerical examples. Moreover, it outperforms the epsilon-greedy strategy in terms of solution quality while demanding only a fraction of the computational resources. This primal-dual algorithm presents an innovative solution to the CMDPs that balances performance with computational affordability. It successfully targets the critical'sample-efficiency' aspect, marking a notable advancement in the literature. Our work has been publicly shared through arXiv, arXiv:2207.014

Additionally, there are two associated documents: arXiv:2207.01409 and arXiv:2207.01410. These documents further detail our research, extending it with additional theoretical and practical findings. Specifically, arXiv:2207.01409 delves into the convergence rates of our dual algorithm, while arXiv:2207.01410 explores more intricate CMDP scenarios with diverse constraint types. These related documents offer enhanced replication materials, allowing for a more comprehensive examination of our research.

By applying a preconditioning matrix and adjusting the transition kernel, we reformulate the on-policy actor-critic reinforcement learning problem, which leads to improved sampling efficiency and faster convergence. This paper presents an innovative method for incorporating sonar technology in an autonomous vehicle's (AV) sensing capabilities. In the context of autonomous driving, a sonar sensor serves as an economical and weather-resistant alternative to more advanced radar and lidar technologies, offering decent range accuracy at a lower cost. However, sonar data is marred by significant variance, which necessitates accurate distortion correction and data filtering to facilitate effective navigation. We address this challenge by developing a novel algorithm that accurately calibrates sonar readings, applies a data filter, and inputs corrected data into the AV's navigation system. Our experimental results showcase significantly improved navigation accuracy with the integrated sonar system, boasting a 35% reduction in lane departure errors and 25% reduction in navigation course adjustments. A new machine learning method is proposed to enhance a patient's health outcome by optimizing the sequence of treatments they receive over time. The approach involves a two-step process. Firstly, a patient's long-term health projection is forecasted by simulating treatment interventions. Secondly, a recommendation policy is identified that maximizes the patient's expected future health, subject to constraints such as adhering to the prescribed treatment sequence. The optimization process is repeated until no further improvements can be made, at which point a Bayesian learning-based algorithm is utilized to refine the model and yield the best treatment recommendations. Simulations and real-world data analyses demonstrate that this method can effectively improve patient outcomes when incorporated into a treatment regimen. Additionally, the approach can reveal valuable insights regarding the most beneficial treatment sequences at different time points. The method can be applied to various settings, such as medicine and marketing, where customers' responses to sequential interventions can evolve over time. Valuable lessons can also be drawn from these applications in the fields of economics and finance. In the absence of disorder, topological superconductivity can occur when chiral fermions occupy a smooth band, rendering the system gapless. We demonstrate that at zero temperature, an infinite number of electron pairs form, achieving a fully paired superconducting state, characterized by a zero gap at zero momentum. Through perturbative and numerical investigations, we establish that this result is robust to both weak disorder and interactions with a Fermi surface, provided the band remains smooth. We further illustrate the emergence of superconductivity through both non-perturbative and numerical exact fermionic functional integrals. In the event of a smooth band, we propose that a fully paired superconducting state can be achieved through the exchange of bosonic modes, such as phonons or other carriers, leading to an electron pair distance of order $1/\kappa$. We show that this scenario is quantitatively consistent with the results obtained from both perturbative and numerical investigations. Lastly, we contend that the underlying mechanism giving rise to superconductivity is analogous to that of BCS theory, with the added provision that the pairing interaction is effective across the entire band due to its smooth nature. Consequently, we expect superconducting delocalization to occur for any number $N$ of electrons. Conversely, we posit that a fully localized zero-gap state can only arise in the presence of disorder. These theoretical predictions are substantiated by numerical data obtained from exact fermionic functional integrations and we propose that these concepts should be experimentally verified in materials such as PtSn and related compounds. Finally, we speculate that the interplay between topological smooth bands, superconductivity, and fermionic superfluidity may give rise to novel behaviors in exotic fermion systems. Researchers employ different methods to identify clusters of sites with similar species compositions. This study compares the performance of six clustering techniques - model-based clustering with Gaussian mixtures, a Bayesian approach, and unsupervised clustering using hierarchical agglomerative methods with the Jaccard, Mahalanobis, and Pearson metrics - on simulated and real datasets. The results show that the Bayesian approach and the model-based clustering method outperformed the other options in simulating a latent cluster structure. However, these two techniques struggled with the challenges of the Pearson data. The hierarchical methods and the Bayesian approach generally performed well on the Pearson data, but struggled with the Bayesian approach when the cluster sizes varied. Ultimately, the best performers were the hierarchical methods with the Jaccard metric and the Bayesian approach on the Pearson data when the cluster sizes were similar. The hierarchical methods with the Mahalanobis metric performed well on the Gaussian presence-absence data, similar to the Bayesian approach and model-based clustering methods. The Bayesian approach outperformed the other options in identifying the hierarchical methods' underlying cluster structures in both the simulated and real datasets. In summary, the Bayesian approach and model-based clustering methods are recommended for analyzing presence-absence data, but the hierarchical methods with the Jaccard metric and the Mahalanobis metric are also effective options, particularly when the data are high-dimensional and the cluster sizes are similar. The R code used in this study is available on GitHub at https://github.com/alexandremoutreau/Comparing_clustering_methods_on_presence-absence_data under the MIT license. We investigate two popular Standard Model extensions, one based on $SU(4)_X \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_C$ and another on $U(1)_X \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$, which are both derived from the $SO(10)$ theory by simplifying certain fermions into scalar fields. Our focus is on the $U(1)_X$ component, which is crucial for generating dark matter and influencing the properties of Higgs and gauge bosons as observed. We thoroughly examine the properties of Higgs bosons, gauge bosons, and dark matter in these models, calculating the masses of $X$ and deriving constraints from direct detection experiments, electroweak precision tests, and the properties of the Higgs boson. We also discuss the naturalness of these models requiring high energy scales, exemplified by the example of $SU(4)_X \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_C$ with extra $SU(2)_C$ and a left-right symmetric model as a low-energy extension. Furthermore, we analyze the stability of the simplest model, which we denote as $\mathcal{M}_{1}$. We find that its stability depends on the values of $\kappa_c$ and $\kappa_L$, which can lead to various lifetimes for the $X$ particle. However, in the case of $\kappa_L \ll \kappa_c$, we find that the $X$ particle decays into a neutrino and an anti-neutrino, which results in visible effects on dark matter relic densities, thereby satisfying the Planck experiment's requirements. On the other hand, in the case of $\kappa_L \gg \kappa_c$, the $X$ particle decays either into a photon and a fermion or undergoes lepton number violation, which could be detected by experiments such as the NA62 long-lived particle search. Finally, we discuss the prospects and challenges of testing these models in future long-lived particle searches, dark matter direct detection experiments, and high-energy colliders. In particular, we find that the $U(1)_X$ model can be tested in the NA62 experiment by searching for rare decays of hadrons into dark matter and anti-matter pairs. Similarly, we find that the $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_X \times U(1)_Y$ model can be tested in the CMS experiment

The DRA bears a resemblance to the Newton-Morse method in continuous optimization and is motivated by an alternative representation of the Nash equilibrium equation. Each iteration of DRA involves solving two distinct linear systems and generating a distorted resolvent using the parameters from these systems. If the parameters converge to a suitable limit, the distorted resolvent converges as well. We prove that under certain conditions, starting from an arbitrary initial point, the DRA generates a sequence whose limit point is a Nash equilibrium. We further enhance the DRA's efficiency by introducing a preconditioning modification, which allows using a distorted resolvent computed in an earlier iteration to solve a linear system. Self-supervised learning in visual transformer models (ViT) has recently gained significant interest, with ViTSSO achieving notable success in extracting meaningful image features without labeled data. Unlike traditional distillation methods, which rely on soft labels, ViTSSO uses a contrastive loss to train a feature map, extracting semantic cues along the way. Our analysis reveals that self-supervised ViTSSO models acquire additional attributes, unrelated to the original data, which become apparent under specialized queries. These emerging attributes are not only extracted during the training process, but also persist even after the original data is removed. Our proposed method capitalizes on these hidden representations, using them to drive attribute-driven semantic segmentation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the emerging attributes can serve as a form of knowledge acquisition, where these previously unseen features can be used to generate novel synthetic data. When combined with label information, these attributes enable high-quality edited images in generative visual manipulation tasks. Ultimately, our findings underscore the versatility of self-supervised learning in ViT, allowing it to discover and extract rich, meaningful features from raw images. Code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/jbostrom/ViT_SSE.

Extensive experiments were conducted with a large weather dataset of 1 million points, and the results demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art models in all three dimensions. This method detects hidden patterns in financial data and identifies the most frequent configurations, which show strong correlation with positive returns. Through a comprehensive study, we examined various parameters such as network scale, price movement thresholds, and return duration to understand their impact on detecting these patterns. Additionally, we demonstrated the stability of our method by comparing it to a traditional statistical approach, showing its accuracy and reliability. This work not only provides a solid theoretical foundation but also a practical tool, called NeMo, for investors to use. A demonstration video and documentation are available online, and NeMo can be downloaded as an open-source software. This innovative approach bridges financial analysis and network science, offering a new perspective to understand and make informed investment decisions in the financial market. Experimental evaluation of NeMo's performance revealed high accuracy and robust results, validating its effectiveness as a tool to detect significant patterns in financial data. A thorough investigation of NeMo's properties and patterns further demonstrated its capabilities and provided insights into its performance. Furthermore, we explored different applications of NeMo, including its use as a standalone tool to provide individual investment advice and combine the method with other techniques, such as technical indicators, to enhance its overall accuracy and decision-making capabilities. This comprehensive research contributes to the development of new methods in network analysis and provides practical solutions for investors to make informed decisions. A thorough examination of NeMo's performance, along with detailed analyses and evaluations, confirm its relevance and importance in the field, paving the way for future research and developments. Specifically, we found that network motifs are capable of detecting significant patterns, and our tool, NeMo, offers a flexible solution with various applications and decision-making capabilities. Furthermore, our study validates the effectiveness of our method and provides a solid foundation for future research in network analysis. Additionally, we have made available a comprehensive dataset containing results from our experiments for further investigation. Our research focuses on analyzing spectral emissions from a white dwarf as it accretes onto a black hole. To achieve this, we employ the relativistic diffusion model and consider synchrotron radiation and its subsequent scattering by electrons, as well as relativistic inversions of photons. A detailed numerical simulation is conducted to calculate gamma-ray emissions, and our findings are compared with observations from the Fermi telescope. Specifically, we examine a particular binary system, PS1830-130, and calculate gamma-ray emissions over a 10-year period. This work enables us to assess whether accretion from a white dwarf to a black hole can be the primary source of high-energy emissions in this system. Furthermore, we are able to derive the efficiency with which the black hole converts accreted matter into radiation. Our analysis indicates that gamma-ray emissions from this process are insufficient to explain the observed levels in the Fermi telescope, although our results do account for some of the variability over the observed period. A parameter that governs the efficiency in our model must also take on a specific value to accommodate this variability. Interestingly, our findings also suggest that X-ray emissions from this process are insufficient to explain the observed levels in this system, and we are able to derive a maximum efficiency for the black hole as it accretes matter from a white dwarf. Our research provides new insights into the physics of this binary system and the black hole itself. This work is part of a larger research project that is reevaluating the role of accretion from a white dwarf to a black hole in explaining high-energy emissions in this system. Our findings are contingent on our understanding of the binary system's motion and its effects on the emissions, as well as the properties of the white dwarf and its effects on the emissions. A full evaluation of this process must consider these factors to provide a complete explanation of the observed high-energy emissions in this system.
