Traditional motion blur removal techniques often struggle to distinguish between movement caused by objects and the camera. Most methods either remove all blur or retain it throughout the image, overlooking crucial details in the process. To overcome this limitation, we've developed an innovative approach that mimics blur production to differentiate between of objects and the surrounding environment. A dynamic, image-specific blur generator is proposed, enabling the separation of moving and stationary objects within an image. A subsequent module then applies de-blurring techniques specifically tailored to each component, resulting in sharper focus on the main subject while maintaining a blurred background. To train this innovative method, we've created a massive 90-million image dataset encompassing a wide range of natural blur effects, allowing the model to learn the underlying principles of blur production. In our experiments, the proposed technique demonstrated superior outcomes, restoring original details in challenging cases like astronomical images and retaining background blur in portraits. The ultrapower of any ordered set is created by applying a specific mapping in a maximally extended sense, and its resulting structure retains an ordered nature. Introducing the notion of entirely ordered sets, we find that this property persists in the first ultrapower and remains inherent in sets with well-ordered chains. Furthermore, the entirely ordered property in a set is equivalent to all its infinite chains being well-ordered within a certain cardinality that is less than $\aleph_1$. Additionally, we establish that a set's realisation in a certain extended structure of real numbers contains entirely ordered substructures if and only if the original set has infinite subsets with cardinalities ranging from $\aleph_0$ to $\aleph_1$. Lastly, we present a categorisation of sets according to the cardinality of entirely ordered substructures within their first ultrapowers. Depending on this cardinality, sets are classified into three groups: those with substructures of cardinality $\aleph_0$, those with substructures of cardinality $\aleph_1$, or those with substructures of cardinality greater than $\aleph_1$. It is noteworthy that a set with substructures of cardinality $\aleph_1$ contains sets with substructures of cardinality $\aleph_0$ as well as sets without such substructures. Similarly, a set without substructures of cardinality $\aleph_1$ contains sets with substructures of cardinality greater than $\aleph_1$ and sets with substructures of cardinality $\aleph_1$. Finally, a set with substructures of cardinality greater than $\aleph_1$ contains sets with substructures of cardinality $\aleph_0$, sets with substructures of cardinality $\aleph_1$, and sets with substructures of cardinality greater than $\aleph_1$. A graph theory hypothesis known as Hadwiger's Conjecture asserts that every graph with t distinct colors contains a subgraph isomorphic to a complete graph with t vertices. We affirm this conjecture for particular instances where the graph with t colors is part of a larger t+1 colored graph, effectively extending an earlier outcome that applied to graphs with 4 colors, to those with 5 colors. The concept of near complete graphs, referring to graphs with almost all possible edges present, plays a significant role in the proof process. The process involves demonstrating the presence of a specific subgraph within a larger graph and then removing certain edges from it to reveal the presence of a complete graph with t vertices within the original graph. The proof relies heavily on an efficient strategy for edge removal, allowing us to confirm the Hadwiger's Conjecture for the given cases. The verification of our approach involved a manual examination of all possible configurations of near complete graphs with 4 and 5 colors to confirm the complete graphs with 4 and 5 vertices within them. This research introduces an innovative framework for accurately reconstructing smooth graph signals, even in the presence of noisy and incomplete measurements. The generalized correntropy between nodes is utilized to create a robust cost function, enabling the derivation of an optimal kernel width that consistently performs well across diverse graph configurations. The resulting optimization problem is tackled using an efficient primal-dual subgradient method, which is analytically defined and proven to converge. The framework's adaptability and convergence of the kernel width in real-time allow it to generalize to any graph signal, without the need for manual kernel width selection. The approach is further demonstrated to be more resilient to measurement noise compared to traditional minimum mean squared error-based methods. Simulation results confirm the framework's accuracy and noise resilience across various scenarios, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in most cases. The framework's effectiveness is substantiated through experimental applications in brain signal decoding and image compression. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/AAli7861-Generalized-Correntropy-based-SGR. The kernel width's analytical expression can be found in Eq. (16), with supporting proofs in the supplementary materials available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11148. The framework's theoretical properties are detailed in Sections 2-5, with numerical results presented in Section 6 and validated by multiple experiments. The framework's name, 'Robust Adaptive Generalized Correntropy-based Smoothed Graph Signal Reconstruction with a Kernel Width Learning', accurately describes the novel approach presented in this research paper. The framework can be summarized as follows: The problem of graph signal reconstruction is approached through the generalized correntropy between nodes, leading to the derivation of an optimal kernel width that consistently performs well across diverse graph configurations. The resulting cost function is optimized using a primal-dual subgradient method, which is analytically defined and proven to converge. The framework converges to the optimal solution, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in most cases due to its adaptability and noise resilience properties. The kernel width is learned in real-time, enabling generalization to any graph signal without manual kernel width selection. The framework's effectiveness is substantiated by simulations, experimental validation, and theoretical properties that guarantee convergence and stability. The framework's name and approach are chosen to highlight its novel aspects and robust performance. In experiments involving entangled particles, the optimal outcome is often hampered by imperfect measurements, due to the simultaneous detection of multiple particles, which can lead to double counting and lost signals. These detection limitations result in the distortion of quantum correlations, ultimately limiting the accuracy of entangled interferometry. We conducted an experiment involving two spin particles, employing a entangled state and multiple measurement settings, to demonstrate how detection noise distorts quantum correlations. We developed an analytical method to characterize and mitigate detection noise, allowing us to recover entangled states and enhance quantum correlations. We successfully implemented this approach and observed the elimination of distortion, effectively generating customized entangled states. The techniques employed in this study can be applied to a range of fields, including precision measurement, quantum information processing, and quantum communication. Additionally, our methods may facilitate the development of sophisticated quantum algorithms and tasks, such as quantum teleportation and secret key distribution, by utilizing entangled states with specific properties. These techniques may also contribute to the advancement of interferometry, by utilizing states with specific structures, such as entanglement in only one component, which can enhance signal output and overcome detection limitations. Furthermore, this research may pave the way for the implementation of entangled quantum computing and communication systems, by utilizing these techniques to generate and control customized entangled states. The study has been published in an article titled "Customized generation of quantum states in an entangled spinor interferometer to overcome detection noise," which can be found at the following arXiv link: arxiv.org/abs/2207.13365. We investigate the first eigenvalue of the first Robin eigenvalue problem for the $p$-Laplace operator. Our research yields precise estimates for the eigenvalue, considering the influence of $p$-harmonic functions and boundary conditions, in addition to dimensional and subharmonic functionery effects. These estimates are precise and valid under minimal assumptions on the free boundary. In contrast to existing eigenvalue theory, these estimates surpass the known lower and upper bounds for the eigenvalue, amounting to $p$-fractional Robin constants. Several examples and edge cases are also explored to illustrate the precision of the estimates and their implications when $p$ approaches or equals one. Furthermore, our findings encompass a special case of the first eigenvalue of $p$-Laplace operators with nonlinear boundary conditions. In this context, we establish an equality for $p$-fractional Adams operators and derive precise estimates for the first eigenvalue of a related problem, involving a nonlinear field equation first investigated by Kusano in the 1960s. Our study generalizes existing results for the first eigenvalue of $p$-Laplace operators, applying to a broader class of functions and providing precise estimates, surpassing existing upper and lower bounds. Several examples and counterexamples are also provided to demonstrate the precision and validity of our estimates and their behavior under specific parameter values. Deep Learning techniques have rapidly expanded in various machine learning applications. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) show significant promise in analyzing complex graph-structured data, although their theoretical foundations are somewhat ambiguous. Unlike common neural networks, GCNNs utilize an opaque and intricately designed architecture that is difficult to grasp. In this study, we reexamine the underlying principles of GCNNs and offer a simplified framework by linking them to a traditional signal processing concept – matched filtering. This intuitive approach enables GCNNs to be viewed as a network of narrowband filters, each addressing a unique node in the graph, thereby extracting distinct signals specific to local neighborhoods and nodes. Consequently, this signal-specific data is combined to derive the node feature. This simplified understanding not only clarifies the GCNN's working mechanism but also offers a systematic approach to model design, as evidenced by experimental results on multiple graph classification benchmarks. Moreover, this approach facilitates reducing the number of model parameters, thereby enhancing the network's interpretability without compromising its performance. Comprehensive code and model configurations are available on GitHub for reproduction of our experimental findings. Additionally, the implemented models can be hosted on remote computing services like Google Colab for easy access and exploratory analysis. This includes visualizing the matched filtering process through signal spectrograms and heatmaps, which demonstrate local signal extraction and the GCNN's graph topology, respectively. These additional resources enable in-depth study of GCNNs and offer a straightforward design methodology for creating GCNN-based models from scratch. Ultimately, our study offers a precise and systematic model design approach that outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, including highly acclaimed architectures like SAMGCN, SAMGNN, DeepGCN, and GraphSAGE. Our study's findings are empirically validated on multiple graph classification benchmark datasets, namely MUTAG, PROTEINS, IMDB-BINARY, YELP, and REDDIT-112K. These benchmarks encompass chemical graph representations and real-world datasets, thereby encompassing a diverse range of applications across chemistry and computer vision. Notably, our study's models exhibit exceptional performance on these benchmark datasets while possessing significantly fewer parameters compared to existing state-of-the-art models. This remarkable performance is attributed to the intuitive matched filtering concept, which enables systematic model design and enhances the network's interpretability. The universal algebra of branes in string theory corresponds to the Borel subalgebra of a quantum group. To capture both reversible and irreversible transformations, we introduce the quantum Branes algebra, an extension of the Borel subalgebra, incorporating factors that account for time and temperature dependencies. Utilizing the principle of duality in conformal field theories, we generate the relevant branching rules, which enable a systematic approach to identifying braanes. This algebraic framework is then applied to study defect lines and their interactions within two-dimensional conformal field theories. Furthermore, we provide evidence that the branes algebra is a quotient of the colored rational part of the principal specialization of the Alexander and HOMFLY-PT polynomials. To validate these claims, we present a geometric interpretation of the branes algebra through a local model that incorporates time and temperature dependencies, specifically adapted from a study of Markov matrices. As a result, the relevance of time and temperature factors is intrinsic to the branes algebra, allowing for the generalization of Reversibility Principle to branes in string theory. This theory is implied by a geometric model that incorporates time and temperature factors, which we propose as a new structure for braanes in string theory. To demonstrate these claims, we first establish the relevance of time and temperature factors to braanes in string theory, which is confirmed through an analysis of the Gopakumar-Vafa invariants. These claims are also validated in tests for random branes and vanishing branes cases. Additionally, we found that the branes algebra is related to a subalgebra of the Ducek algebra, which is a quantization of the Novikov prime series. Finally, we found that braanes in string theory are related to Gopakumar-Vafa invariants through a duality principle, which is confirmed through an analysis of random branes and vanishing branes cases. These relationships between braanes, duality principles, and the Reversibility Principle are fundamental properties of string theory, as predicted by a geometric model that incorporates time and temperature dependencies. These claims are confirmed through a re-examination of the known results on braanes, which demonstrate how the Reversibility Principle can be generalized to braanes in string theory. In support of these claims, we present a new geometric model for braanes in string theory, which is based on a local time and temperature dependent adaptation of the branes algebra. This model maintains the fundamental properties of the Reversibility Principle, while accurately describing both reversible and irreversible transformations,

Achieving a Lipschitz selection for a set-valued mapping $F:\mathbb{R}^n\rightrightarrows\mathbb{R}^n$ with minimal Hausdorff dimension less than 2 is now understood to be a solvable optimization problem, which has specific criteria for a low-dimensional mapping $F$. The problem can be reduced to finding a metric intermediate surface - a surface whose normal vector points towards the mapping's graph - using a metric that is compatible with $F$. The normal vector's metric properties allow us to derive necessary conditions for $F$ to have a Lipschitz selection, which includes it being a Lipschitz $\alpha$-selection for some $\alpha<2$. The conditions also imply that the mapping's graph must be a Lipschitz manifold - a structure that provides local representations and properties of the mapping's metric curvature. The optimization problem's solution provides a pathway to determine if a set-valued mapping on a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ has a Lipschitz selection. The general approach to achieving a Lipschitz selection has been extended to obtaining a semismooth van der Waerden domain - a concept applied in solving a generalized van der Waerden problem. The efficiency of this method has been demonstrated through numerical examples, which also showcase its potential for use in many other applications, including constructing metric $L^p$-approximations and the van der Waerden problem itself. The techniques employed to analyze the optimization problem involve using normal surfaces and vector fields to dissect the mapping's metric properties and the mappings that possess Lipschitz selections. The methods used draw parallels with established results - for example, the integration theorems and Bruck's metric interpolation theorem. The results obtained generalize and integrate various concepts and results, including those for set-valued mappings with low Hausdorff dimension, which is equivalent to low metric box dimension. The concepts and properties derived apply to any set-valued mapping on a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$, which includes those that are not Lipschitz continuous but possess local Lipschitz selections, which implies they have a certain metric smoothness. This research investigates how the compile-time set-up phase can optimize and customize the run-time environment of a program. An experimental language, RLS, was developed to mimic the core properties of a C-like language and support arbitrary compile-time environments. An in-depth study of optimizing the run-time behavior of RLS programs via compile-time transformations was conducted, focusing on four key areas: dynamic memory allocation, data structure indexing, string manipulation, and pattern matching. The findings demonstrate that meaningful optimizations can be applied to the run-time behavior of programs during the compile-time phase, resulting in substantial performance improvements amounting to up to 3 times the original execution speed, with some specific cases even achieving run-time efficiencies comparable to manually optimized code. This research presents a novel approach to specializing the run-time setup space at compile-time. The study also highlights key challenges and stimulates further exploration in this area, including opacity in dynamic data structures, and sets the stage for future research in this domain. Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals is critical in assessing heart function, yet accurate estimation remains challenging due to signal noise. Researchers have developed various methods to estimate IBIs, including those based on machine learning, but many of these approaches remain inaccessible because they require specialized training. In an effort to overcome this limitation, a recent study introduced an innovative, easy-to-implement neural network called the Tiramisu model, which effectively estimates IBIs from raw ECG signals with reduced estimation errors. The study showcases the feasibility of using the Tiramisu model to monitor heart function in elderly care centers via mobile devices. Furthermore, the estimated IBIs can be used to calculate the NN80, NN20, and SDNN indices, which provide valuable insights into autonomic nervous system dysfunction and overall cardiovascular risk. To validate the Tiramisu model, the researchers conducted extensive testing using multiple datasets, including the MIT-BIH arrhythmia dataset and records from patients with atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, and valve disease. The results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses traditional estimation methods while being simpler and more versatile. Consequently, the Tiramisu model presents a viable option for accurately estimating IBIs and calculating cardiovascular risk indices from raw ECG signals with reduced errors. Due to its ease of implementation, this model has numerous clinical applications and can be used for monitoring cardiovascular disease in various patient populations. Given its moderate computational requirements, the method can be used on mobile devices, enabling real-time monitoring of heart function and cardiovascular risk in elderly care centers and other outpatient settings. A Python code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/RafaelZaiat/Estimation-IBI-Tiramis. The proposed method has been tested and validated according to the standards established by the PhysioNet Challenge 2019. A comprehensive description of the challenge, including participating algorithms and results, can be found in the competition webpage at https://physionet.stanford.edu/physiohtml/2019/physionet-challenge-2019.html. A freely downloadable ECG signal dataset is available at https://physionet.stanford.edu/. This work has been supported by grants from the Brazilian institutions CAPES, CNPq, and FAPEL. We're taking a novel approach to this issue by designing a task-independent framework that leverages a general task representation to guide the translation of a classifier from a high-resource language to a low-resource one.  This translation is achieved through two stages: one that produces a task-neutral prototype from the source language, and another that maps it to the target language.  Our method takes full advantage of both task and language similarities without imposing any additional structure.  We've implemented a neural network to implement this framework and evaluated it on three datasets for sentiment analysis, resulting in accurate predictions on previously unlabeled languages.  For instance, the system can take a Spanish sentiment classifier and use it to predict sentiments for sentences in Portuguese, a language without corresponding labels. In this paper, we prove a modified version of the three balls conjecture for functions that are solutions to the Dirac equation in n-dimensional Euclidean space, where n is greater than or equal to three. This is based on specific assumptions about the function's behavior at its origin and its decay outside of a given ball. We establish that the ball that contains the origin accounts for the majority of the function's total 'energy', and that this result can be extended to functions that are nearly homogeneous with a power law that decreases at an adequate rate. This finding is then compared with existing research on this topic. Additionally, this proof relies on an alternative approach that involves a complex variable method, as described in the paper's body, which avoids the reliance on 'proxy functions' that are present in previous proofs. This allows us to derive precise estimates of the function's behavior and its 'energy' within a specified region, ultimately yielding a more precise understanding of the three balls conjecture in this context. Furthermore, this method holds promise for the extension and application to other problems in analysis and physics. This result is then complemented by a related finding in the paper, which provides a precise upper limit on the function's 'energy' within a specified region, along with a relevant comparison with existing research on this topic. This work is then concluded by speculating on potential applications and extensions of this result in the fields of physics and number theory. This research is particularly relevant due to the connections between the dirac operator, monogenic functions, and solutions to elliptic equations that are present in various frameworks of physics and engineering. As a consequence, this result holds not only in the Euclidean space but also in any rotatable domain in n-dimensional space. This paper introduces the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet model, an advanced generative network based on Autoregressive Raw Waveform Models. By integrating Pitch-dependent Expanded Convolution Neural Network (PDECNN) with WaveNet, the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet effectively captures complex patterns in speech at various scales. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Quasi-Periodic WaveNet achieves superior quality compared to the standard WaveNet, at a significantly lower computational cost. Additionally, the model exhibits greater efficiency in terms of training time and required data examples. Our findings show that the Quasi-Periodic WaveNet achieves a higher Viterbi score of 0.9526 and a lower computational cost of 0.87, indicating a 17% reduction in computational expense with only a 0.02% Viterbi score degradation. Furthermore, the model displays a greater degree of consistency in generated speech under different sampling rates, outperforming the WaveNet model with a sampling score of 0.995 and a mean absolute error of 2.14 samples. Latin America's largest conference on artificial intelligence, the Brazilian Conference on Intelligent Systems, took place in São Paulo this year, featuring an impressive judging panel led by Dr. Jose Manuel Mendez, and including ourselves, along with Dr. Carlos Eduardo, Dr. Alberto Sanchez, and Dr. Qiu Ji, as its reviewers. Our paper, titled "Bivalent Matrix Factorization: A Bayesian Approach with Biclusters", has been selected for publication in the conference's proceedings through a rigorous peer-review process. This abstract outlines the key points of our research. Large-scale recommender systems face significant data sparsity issues, causing substantial overhead in computing user preferences, thus highlighting the need to leverage environmental cues from nearby users to fill in missing ratings. To this end, we propose the Bivalent Matrix Factorization with Biclusters (BMB) method, which models users and items within the context of community-specific groups to exploit shared patterns in their behavior. Users are grouped based on consistent patterns of interaction within these communities, and the latent factors representing their preferences are identified through the analysis of their intra-group engagement. To capture item-specific characteristics and accommodate subjective opinions, we also introduce a diagonal matrix to model random fluctuations in user ratings. Experimentation using two real-world datasets reveals that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art collaborative filtering techniques, specifically surpassing the performance of the widely successful Latent Factor Model in both accuracy and speed. Moreover, our novel bicluster-based model offers valuable insights into user communities by clustering users and identifying item categories in a meaningful and interpretable manner. Finally, the incorporation of random preferences enables the capture of unique, subjective aspects of user preferences, thus facilitating the recommendation of distinct and personalized items. In summary, our BMB method offers an efficient and effective means of learning user preferences from sparse and noisy data by modeling their behavior within the context of community-specific groups, thus revealing a range of new theoretical and practical insights for recommender systems. It also opens up the potential for related innovations in natural language processing and computer vision by extending the bicluster-based models originally developed in image analysis. Ultimately, this approach can be used to develop a variety of intelligent systems for interacting with the world around us, thus enabling a deeper and more intuitive connection between humans, computers, and the environment. Magnetic activity in the Sun has significant spectral variations that affect its spectral properties.  By using the HARPS-N solar telescope, researchers have made extensive observations of the Sun, spanning a wide range of magnetic activity levels.  In this study, we investigate the impact of magnetic activity on the Sun's spectral properties and identify reliable indicators among the observed spectral features.  By analyzing the data, we find that several indicators including the core weakness of the Ca II infrared band and spectrographic solar indices show consistent correlations with magnetic activity levels.  We also explore new activity indicators and compare their robustness in predicting the solar luminosity due to magnetic activity, ultimately identifying the most reliable indicators among the observed spectral features.  These indicators have the potential to accurately determine the luminosity of other solar-type stars based on their spectral characteristics.  Additionally, we find that the SMI (Solar Magnetic Indicators) activity index is the most reliable in predicting the solar luminosity, followed by the CSI (Solar Magnetic Index), with other indicators showing varying correlations depending on the magnetic activity levels.  Our results provide insights into the spectral features of stars with known activity levels, and the relationships between magnetic activity, spectral features, and luminosity can help identify the most reliable indicators for determining the stellar luminosity in solar-type stars.  Furthermore, we have established a relationship between magnetic activity and the spectral feature at 450.1 nm, and the resulting empirical formula can predict the spectral feature in inactive stars.  Our research data, including raw and processed data, are available at the URL https://doi.org/10.1781/GeSCI-DTZA-SS. This approach involves exposing the system to the influence of ohmic dissipation through a resistive contact, which should preferentially eliminate the Majorana peak due to its fragile zero-mode state. Numerical simulations of the resulting spectroscopy have shown that the presence of ohmic dissipation causes the Majorana peak to shrink while the ordinary peak remains largely unaffected, which is in line with theoretical predictions. Furthermore, we found that the transport rate and spectral shift induced by the ohmic coupling are highly dependent on the ratio of the coupling strength to the lever arm of the resistive contact. These outcomes demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately distinguish the Majorana peak from other peaks through visible changes in its shape and position. This innovative strategy could provide a practical means for identifying Majorana modes in realistic systems. Additionally, we applied and validated our method against a variety of scenarios characterized by different values of the lever arm and coupling strength, which are common variables influencing the behavior of Majorana modes in diverse systems. This analysis has further underscored the potential of our method to identify Majorana modes in a wide range of systems. Lastly, we explored the applicability of our method to systems where the transport is facilitated not by a resistive contact but by a gate electrode, which carries a charge. A multi-task learning approach was employed, simultaneously predicting engagement and content metadata such as view count, liking, and commenting. For view count, a linear transformation was used, whereas binary variables like liking and commenting were predicted using the logistic function. The intricate patterns formed on snow-covered ground, known as snow crystals, are a result of the complex interaction between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake growth.  Despite being a major component of the snow's morphology, the specific influence of turbulence remains poorly understood.  Research has shown that large snowflakes are broken down by turbulent eddies, but the effect of smaller eddies on the snowflakes is still a subject of study.  In our research, a high-speed camera was used to capture high-definition footage of snowflakes falling through a turbulent air flow in a laboratory setting.  By using advanced image processing, the behavior of individual snowflakes could be tracked as they passed through the turbulent air. A novel, biologically inspired approach to robot locomotion is presented, drawing motivation and encouragement from the unique climbing abilities of the Pacific Lamprey. A robot designed in accordance with the lamprey's slender body shape and undulating body movement has demonstrated successful testing on soft, inclined surfaces made of silicone. The robot's body is divided into separate sections that contract in a synchronized manner to propel it forward. A control system incorporating time-delayed feedback and prosthetic neural forces has been implemented to simulate the lamprey's central pattern generator, producing the desired undulating motion. As a result, the robot has demonstrated the capacity to move at 8 cm per second on a 20-degree incline. A study on the dynamic system behind the Pacific Lamprey's locomotion has been carried out, feeding data into an optimal control problem that maximizes the robot's efficiency and stability. A suitable control law has been derived through optimal control calculations and put into practice on the robot, at which point the following outcomes were observed: the robot can achieve an angle of the body for optimal descent and maintain a stable, straight body position when static. The derived control law has greatly improved the robot's speed to 24 cm per second on a 20-degree incline and has given the robot enhanced stability and efficiency. A comparison of the Pacific Lamprey-inspired robot's performance with other robots from similar fields has been conducted, revealing its superiority in a variety of metrics. A Pacific Lamprey-inspired robot has also demonstrated its ability to navigate a complex 3D terrain using its unique locomotion abilities. As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into daily life, its ability to provide accurate and trustworthy predictions depends heavily on high-quality requirements that prioritize user understanding. However, the AI development process often disregards user-centric considerations, leading to prioritization of technical complexities over user needs. The emergence of explainable AI (XAI) aims to enhance trust in AI systems by promoting transparency and accountability through human-centered approaches. Since users of AI systems rely heavily on comprehension, the requirements engineering (RE) community can play a vital supportive role in shaping the XAI user experience. Unfortunately, the RE community is not extensively involved in addressing XAI requirements. To bridge this gap, we propose a collaborative framework that harmonizes RE and XAI principles to develop a user-centric approach to explainable AI. Accurate diagnosis and management of colorectal polyps heavily rely on the examination of histological slides, which typically contain detailed descriptions of the specimen's histological features in the accompanying patient records. Despite the significance of these features, they remain largely unquantified and thus unsuitable for machine learning-based analysis. To address this limitation, we have developed UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 3477 histological whole-slide images, along with corresponding annotations that quantify the area affected by specific histopathological features. This dataset is designed to support researchers in developing and training machine learning models to classify colorectal polyps into benign and malignant subtypes, as well as to develop quantitative measures of abnormality to inform adenoma grading in the clinic. To showcase the potential of this dataset, we have contributed two computational tasks: the Colorectal Polyp Classification task and the Adenoma Classification task, which are now included in the PathoChallenge 2022 competition hosted during MICCAI 2022. Further information about UniToPatho, as well as the accompanying software to access the dataset, is available at https://unito-patho.github.io. The dataset can be accessed via the following link: https://unito-patho.github.io/download.html. One of the most successful variational algorithms for solving combinatorial optimization problems is Quantum Alternating Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). However, determining the optimal tuning parameters for QAOA remains an open challenge. We introduce a Bayesian approach to determine the optimal tuning parameters for QAOA variations used to tackle the MaxCut problem. Our method reconstructs the distribution of optimal tuning parameters conditional on the algorithm's performance. By integrating Bayes' rule with simulations of QAOA's behavior, the posterior distribution is refined. From this analysis, the mean and confidence intervals of the optimal tuning parameters can be calculated, enabling their practical utilization. We further adapt and demonstrate this method on physical quantum processors to determine the optimal tuning parameters for the MaxCut problem. Consequently, the algorithm yields improved results with reduced variability. We also discover that the posterior distribution converges to a Gaussian distribution as the number of simulations approaches the classical limit defined by the Shannon number. Consequently, the algorithm's performance becomes predictable and nearly optimal in such a scenario. Furthermore, we investigate the applicability of our method to determine the optimal tuning parameters for near-term quantum machines and reveal that these devices can perform tasks beyond the reach of classical computers due to their ability to exploit quantum speedup. Ultimately, the Bayesian approach presents a valuable tool for achieving practical quantum computing. In particular, we demonstrate improved results for the MaxCut problem on both simulators and actual quantum processors using our method, the details of which we document in our work. We believe that this approach will contribute significantly to the development of reliable quantum computing in the near term. The focus of this paper is to explore the problem of finding the overlap area between two ellipses, which presents complex mathematical challenges. A specific scenario is investigated where one ellipse is partially or entirely contained within another. The key concept of this study is the combination of the generalized intersection area formula and the region splitting method. These methods calculate the overlap area by dividing the region into simpler shapes, such as circles and sectors, and then assessing the bounds of the resulting geometry. The study also examines boundary conditions, which arise when one ellipse is completely enclosed within the other. A numerical approach is developed to estimate the overlap area in cases that cannot be resolved analytically. The proposed methods demonstrate high efficiency, with processing times under 1 microsecond for ellipse dimensions in the range of 10 to 500. The results are validated through visualizations and statistical tests that show the methods to be highly accurate, with error rates of less than 0.03%. The study further considers the scenario of generating random distributions of overlapping circles and analyzing their characteristics. The associated source code is provided for further exploration. A statistical analysis of the results reveals that the area of one ellipse partially covering another follows a normal distribution, whereas the area of one ellipse completely enclosed within another adheres to a log-normal distribution. The study also finds that the proposed region splitting method generates more accurate estimates of the overlap area than alternative approaches. Furthermore, the research shows that the boundary condition, which arises when one ellipse is completely enclosed within the other, can be precisely calculated when the difference in their semi-major axes is less than 10 times the difference in their semi-minor axes. Lastly, the study finds that the overlap area can be accurately estimated down to a precision of 10^-6 in 99.99% of cases, which presents a challenging mathematical problem to solve this level of precision. Accurate vertebrae localization and identification are crucial in various medical applications related to spine pathology. However, certain anatomical variations (e.g., vertebral body shape and size differences, scoliosis) complicate the process and reduce the reliability of existing methods. To address these issues, we have developed a fully automated CT-based approach for locating and identifying vertebrae, taking into account the unique anatomy of the spine. By transforming the sagittally scanned spine into a coronal orientation, our method preserves axial images and enables the use of a L1-regularized least-squares optimization framework to identify vertebrae. The approach relies on constrained vertebrae positioning to accurately calculate the positions of all vertebrae, from the occiput to the sacrum. To evaluate its effectiveness, we tested our approach on two publicly available datasets (SHP and Spine), demonstrating its superiority to other state-of-the-art methods in both datasets. The source code for our method is available at https://github.com/ikorzhov/LBPO. Evaluation results and datasets can be found at https://ikorzhov.github.io/VertebralLBPO/. The fundamental principles of stationary nonequilibrium statistical mechanics were established under the assumption of microscopic system detail by Dobson, Blyth, Esposito, and Junginger in a series of papers. We take this approach a step further by relaxing this assumption and developing a more general framework. This involves applying the theory of Markovian jumps to systems in contact with multiple heat and work reservoirs. Under the presence of multiple heat reservoirs, a unique current field is introduced, whose statistical properties are shown to be invariant to any change in gauge. This concept is applied to the analysis of fluctuation theorems, and a new proof is provided for the fluctuation-dissipation relation, along with a general method for deriving the Gaussian distribution of stationary currents. This framework is compatible with both classical and quantum mechanics. Furthermore, we demonstrate the correctness of the underlying mathematical formalism by showing that our approach reproduces the existing results of Dobson, Blyth, Esposito, and Junginger for single-component systems and multi-component systems. Additionally, we apply our framework to analyze a clasp molecule undergoing simulations in contact with two heat reservoirs. Our analysis successfully verifies the correctness of the fluctuation-dissipation relation and the Gaussian distribution of stationary currents in this complex many-body system. This confirms the wide applicability of our framework to a broad range of physical systems. In a companion paper, we will show that this general framework can be reduced to the semi-invariant approach of thermodynamic uncertainty calculus developed by Blyth, Dobson, Esposito, Junginger, and O'Callaghan. This reveals a previously unrecognized connection between the two approaches, along with providing a new and general proof of the Gaussian distribution of stationary currents. This proof is shown to be universally applicable to any Markovian jump system, regardless of its underlying mechanics. Consequently, the fluctuation-dissipation relation and Gaussian distribution of stationary currents we derive are universally applicable to any systems modeled by sequential Markovian jumps on any state space. This reveals a previously unrecognized wide applicability of the thermodynamic uncertainty calculus approach. This approach can be applied in numerous fields, including biochemistry, nanotechnology, and quantum transport, for predicting the probabilistic outcomes of nonequilibrium processes. These predictions include the likelihood of observing particular currents, the distribution of work done on or by a given system, and the likelihood of observing particular rates of change in a given observable. This approach is inspired by an earlier strategy proposed by N. Schindler and A. Suciu in 2020. The novel contribution of this article is a detailed mathematical analysis in multiple dimensions, building on their one-dimensional findings. In addition, we provide a brief review of relevant concepts in Milnor fibers, cohomology and Lefschetz mixed Hukuhara-Kawai-Koyanagi, along with an exploration of the properties of the critical locus. These calculations result in the creation of a formal power series, which reflects the cohomology classes of the intermediate mixed Hukuhara-Kawai-Koyanigi spaces. Ultimately, we demonstrate that this series is coherent, defining the coherence of the fiber. The article concludes with a discussion of several significant consequences and possible extensions of this theorem. Specifically, we relate the degrees of the Milnor fiber cohomology classes to the degrees of the Lefschetz mixed Hukuhara-Kawai-Koyanigi spaces and the Milnor number, along with an examination of the implications for curves and surfaces.
